A big tornado can disrupt daily life in minutes. The destruction is immediate, but the stress often grows after the storm, when families face unsafe rooms, spoiled food, lost cooling, and long outages. For owners of larger homes, recovery is often harder because the house depends on more systems to stay safe and comfortable. That is why tornado history matters. It shows how destructive these storms can be, how big can a tornado get in extreme cases, and why home preparation needs to start well before the next warning.

![Image 3: White electric car in a garage with a sleek wall-mounted battery and stone driveway.](https://enterprise-service-eu-cdn.ecoflow.com/configurable/images/1774602602754/%E5%A4%A7%E5%AE%B6%E5%82%A8%E5%9C%BA%E6%99%AF%E5%9B%BE42-%E8%BD%A6%E5%85%85.jpg)

## What Were the 10 Worst Tornadoes in US History?

These ten disasters still stand out because of the lives lost, the communities hit, and the scale of destruction left behind. Each big tornado on this list points to the same hard truth: violent storms can overwhelm a town long before people feel ready for them.

2 Great Natchez Tornado 1840 Mississippi 317
3 Great St. Louis Tornado 1896 Missouri, Illinois 255
4 Tupelo Tornado 1936 Mississippi 216

6 Woodward Tornado 1947 Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas 181
7 Joplin Tornado 2011 Missouri 158
8 Amite and Purvis Tornado 1908 Louisiana, Mississippi 143

**_Source:_****_NOAA NCEI, U.S. Tornadoes | Deadliest Tornadoes_**

### 1. Tri-State Tornado

The **Tri-State Tornado** struck on **March 18, 1925**, and tore across parts of **Missouri, Illinois, and Indiana**. It remains the deadliest tornado in U.S. history, with **695 deaths**. Many people still ask what is the deadliest tornado in us history, and the answer is the Tri-State Tornado. What made this big tornado especially terrifying was its long path and relentless speed. It moved through multiple towns in a single afternoon and left entire neighborhoods in ruins. Families had almost no time to react, and many communities had little protection against a storm of that scale. Even today, the Tri-State Tornado stands as the clearest example of how one violent tornado can devastate several states in just a few hours.

### 2. Great Natchez Tornado

The **Great Natchez Tornado** hit **Mississippi** on **May 6, 1840**, and **killed****317 people**. It remains one of the deadliest tornado disasters ever recorded in the United States. The storm struck at a time when warning systems, emergency planning, and storm shelters were almost nonexistent, which left people highly exposed once conditions turned violent. Its death toll also reflected how difficult recovery could be in that era, when transportation, communication, and medical care were far more limited. The Natchez tornado still holds a major place in U.S. weather history because it shows how deadly a powerful tornado can be when people have little chance to prepare.

### 3. Great St. Louis Tornado

The **Great St. Louis Tornado** struck **Missouri and Illinois in 1896** and **killed 255 people**. It became one of the worst urban tornado disasters in American history because it hit a major city and surrounding areas packed with homes, businesses, and public spaces. A big tornado in an urban setting creates a different kind of danger. Falling brick, shattered glass, collapsing structures, and blocked streets can turn a fast-moving storm into a citywide emergency within minutes. The St. Louis tornado showed how quickly heavy damage spreads when violent winds move through a dense population center with little time for escape.

### 4. Tupelo Tornado

The **Tupelo Tornado** hit **Mississippi**on **April 5, 1936**, and **killed 216 people**. It remains one of the deadliest tornadoes ever to strike the South. The storm moved through residential areas where many homes were not built to withstand violent winds, which made the destruction even worse. In places with dense neighborhoods and limited shelter options, a tornado can cause enormous losses in a very short time. The Tupelo disaster is still remembered because it showed that the Deep South faces serious tornado risk, even though many people often picture tornado disasters as a Plains problem first.

### 5. Gainesville Tornado

The **Gainesville Tornado** struck **Georgia** on **April 6, 1936**, and **killed 203 people**. It tore through the heart of a busy business district filled with workers and shoppers, which helps explain why the death toll was so high. When a tornado hits a downtown area during working hours, the damage extends far beyond buildings. It can shut down factories, destroy stores, injure large groups of people at once, and leave a lasting economic wound in the community. Gainesville remains one of the most severe tornado disasters in the Southeast and a strong reminder of how destructive a big tornado can be in a crowded commercial center.

### 6. Woodward Tornado

The **Woodward Tornado** moved across parts of **Texas, Oklahoma, and Kansas** in **1947** and **killed 181 people**. It remains one of the deadliest Plains tornadoes ever recorded. This storm is often remembered for the way it kept producing destruction across a broad stretch of land rather than focusing on just one town. That kind of long-track damage creates a wider regional crisis because emergency response, medical care, and recovery needs all spread across multiple communities at once. The Woodward tornado also reinforced the danger of a big tornado in open country, where storms can travel far and still strike towns with full force.

### 7. Joplin Tornado

The **Joplin Tornado** struck **Missouri** on **May 22, 2011**, and **killed 158 people**. It showed that even in the modern era, a violent tornado can still cause catastrophic losses when it cuts through a populated city. This big tornado injured over 1,000 people and damaged homes, schools, businesses, and medical facilities across a large section of Joplin. Its impact went far beyond the first day because so much of the city’s daily life was disrupted at once. Joplin remains one of the most important modern examples of how severe tornado damage can overwhelm a community even when forecasts and public warnings are available.

### 8. Amite and Purvis Tornado

The **Amite and Purvis Tornado** crossed parts of **Louisiana and Mississippi** in **1908** and **killed 143 people**. It remains one of the deadliest tornadoes ever recorded in the Deep South. The storm is especially important in tornado history because it reminds people that violent tornadoes are not limited to the central Plains. In rural and wooded areas, the danger can be even harder to judge because visibility is poor and warnings may reach people later. The Amite and Purvis tornado also showed how scattered communities can suffer very high losses when a strong storm moves through places with limited shelter and weaker construction.

### 9. New Richmond Tornado

The **New Richmond Tornado** hit **Wisconsin** in **1899** and **killed 117 people**. It devastated the town and left a deep mark on local history. One reason this tornado is still remembered is that it showed how a powerful storm can turn a smaller community into the center of a national disaster story. A violent tornado does not need a large city to produce extreme destruction. In a small town, damage to homes, shops, public buildings, and basic services can affect nearly everyone at once. The New Richmond tornado remains a strong reminder that tornado risk reaches well beyond the areas people most often associate with severe storms.

### 10. Flint-Beecher Tornado

The **Flint-Beecher Tornado** struck **Michigan** in **1953** and **killed 116 people**. For decades, it was the last U.S. tornado to kill more than 100 people, until Joplin in 2011. The storm hit a suburban area, which made its impact especially striking. Many people tend to picture a big tornado crossing farmland or open Plains country, yet this disaster showed how dangerous violent tornadoes can be in developed residential areas as well. Homes, schools, roads, and neighborhood infrastructure can all be hit in a matter of minutes. Flint-Beecher still stands as a warning that suburban communities are never outside tornado risk.

## How to Prepare for the Next Tornado at Home

After a big tornado, families often find that the emergency keeps unfolding long after the wind stops. A strong home plan needs to cover the few minutes before impact and the long hours or days that follow.

Larger homes **need extra attention** because daily life depends on more rooms, more equipment, and usually a heavier electric load. People often ask what states are in tornado alley in the US, but serious tornado risk is not limited to one part of the country. That is why it makes sense to prepare early, even if tornadoes are not seen as a major local threat.

### Choose the Best Shelter Space Early

A tornado warning leaves very little time to decide where to go. The safest option is a safe room, basement, storm cellar, or a small interior room on the lowest level away from windows. In a larger home, it helps to settle that choice early and keep shoes, flashlights, chargers, medications, helmets, and basic first aid supplies close to that space.

### Use More Than One Warning Method

Outdoor sirens can help, though they should never be the only way your household learns about a storm. Phones, weather radio, local television, and local radio all matter, especially at night or when family members are spread across different parts of a large house. A big tornado can move fast, so losing one alert channel should not leave your home blind.

### Keep Supplies Where You Can Reach Them Fast

Emergency supplies work best when they are easy to grab. Water, shelf-stable food, batteries, power banks, pet supplies, sanitation items, and copies of insurance records should be stored where people can reach them quickly under stress. If your household includes children, older adults, or anyone with medical needs, those items should be prepared with the same urgency as food and water.

### Prepare for a Long Outage

A big tornado can take down lines, transformers, roads, and communications across a wide area. In a larger home, the impact grows because safety and comfort often depend on multiple refrigerators, freezers, internet service, security systems, medical devices, well pumps, sump pumps, garage access, and part of the cooling system. That is why outage planning should include a written list of the loads your home cannot lose. A big tornado can leave a large home dealing with far more than storm damage. Food storage, cooling, internet, security, water-related equipment, and key household systems may all depend on stable backup power during a long outage. That is why planning ahead matters. Start by identifying the loads your home cannot lose, then review whether your current setup can support them. ## FAQs

### Q1: What has been the deadliest tornado in US history?

The deadliest tornado in U.S. history was the Tri-State Tornado of March 18, 1925. It killed 695 people as it tore across parts of Missouri, Illinois, and Indiana. It still holds the highest death toll ever recorded for a single tornado event in the United States, which is why it remains central to every discussion of historic tornado disasters.

### Q2: Is an EF5 stronger than an F5?

**No**. An EF5 is not simply stronger than an F5. The two ratings come from different tornado scales. F5 belongs to the original Fujita scale, while EF5 belongs to the Enhanced Fujita scale introduced later. Both represent the highest rating on their own systems, but the EF scale uses updated damage indicators and a revised method for estimating wind strength.

### Q3: How long can a tornado-related power outage last?

Tornado-related power outages can last anywhere **from a few hours to several days**, depending on the severity of the storm, the level of damage to local power lines, and how quickly utility crews can restore service. In areas hit by major tornadoes, some households may be without electricity for an extended period. That is why large homes often benefit from a backup plan that can keep essential systems running, such as refrigeration, lighting, communication devices, and HVAC support when needed.

### Q4: Should you go to the basement during a tornado?

**Yes**. A basement is one of the safest places to shelter during a tornado because it puts more walls and flooring between you and flying debris. If there is no basement, move to a small interior room on the lowest floor, away from windows. Safe rooms and storm shelters offer even stronger protection when they are available.

### Q5: Should large homes prepare for long power outages after a tornado?

**Yes**. Large homes should prepare for long outages because power loss after a tornado can affect far more than lighting. Refrigeration, cooling, internet service, security systems, medical equipment, well pumps, sump pumps, and garage access may all become urgent needs. That is why tornado preparation for larger homes should include both safe shelter planning and [whole-home backup planning](https://us.ecoflow.com/collections/whole-home-backup-power-solutions).

# Top 10 Worst Tornadoes in US History and How to Get Ready

EcoFlow 2026/3/27

A big tornado can disrupt daily life in minutes. The destruction is immediate, but the stress often grows after the storm, when families face unsafe rooms, spoiled food, lost cooling, and long outages. For owners of larger homes, recovery is often harder because the house depends on more systems to stay safe and comfortable. That is why tornado history matters. It shows how destructive these storms can be, how big can a tornado get in extreme cases, and why home preparation needs to start well before the next warning.

## What Were the 10 Worst Tornadoes in US History?

These ten disasters still stand out because of the lives lost, the communities hit, and the scale of destruction left behind. Each big tornado on this list points to the same hard truth: violent storms can overwhelm a town long before people feel ready for them.

**Rank****Tornado****Year****Main Area****Deaths**
1 Tri-State Tornado 1925 Missouri, Illinois, Indiana 695
2 Great Natchez Tornado 1840 Mississippi 317
3 Great St. Louis Tornado 1896 Missouri, Illinois 255
4 Tupelo Tornado 1936 Mississippi 216
5 Gainesville Tornado 1936 Georgia 203
6 Woodward Tornado 1947 Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas 181
7 Joplin Tornado 2011 Missouri 158
8 Amite and Purvis Tornado 1908 Louisiana, Mississippi 143
9 New Richmond Tornado 1899 Wisconsin 117
10 Flint-Beecher Tornado 1953 Michigan 116

**_Source:_****_NOAA NCEI, U.S. Tornadoes | Deadliest Tornadoes_**

### 1. Tri-State Tornado

The **Tri-State Tornado** struck on **March 18, 1925**, and tore across parts of **Missouri, Illinois, and Indiana**. It remains the deadliest tornado in U.S. history, with **695 deaths**. Many people still ask what is the deadliest tornado in us history, and the answer is the Tri-State Tornado. What made this big tornado especially terrifying was its long path and relentless speed. It moved through multiple towns in a single afternoon and left entire neighborhoods in ruins. Families had almost no time to react, and many communities had little protection against a storm of that scale. Even today, the Tri-State Tornado stands as the clearest example of how one violent tornado can devastate several states in just a few hours.

### 2. Great Natchez Tornado

The **Great Natchez Tornado** hit **Mississippi** on **May 6, 1840**, and **killed****317 people**. It remains one of the deadliest tornado disasters ever recorded in the United States. The storm struck at a time when warning systems, emergency planning, and storm shelters were almost nonexistent, which left people highly exposed once conditions turned violent. Its death toll also reflected how difficult recovery could be in that era, when transportation, communication, and medical care were far more limited. The Natchez tornado still holds a major place in U.S. weather history because it shows how deadly a powerful tornado can be when people have little chance to prepare.

### 3. Great St. Louis Tornado

The **Great St. Louis Tornado** struck **Missouri and Illinois in 1896** and **killed 255 people**. It became one of the worst urban tornado disasters in American history because it hit a major city and surrounding areas packed with homes, businesses, and public spaces. A big tornado in an urban setting creates a different kind of danger. Falling brick, shattered glass, collapsing structures, and blocked streets can turn a fast-moving storm into a citywide emergency within minutes. The St. Louis tornado showed how quickly heavy damage spreads when violent winds move through a dense population center with little time for escape.

### 4. Tupelo Tornado

The **Tupelo Tornado** hit **Mississippi**on **April 5, 1936**, and **killed 216 people**. It remains one of the deadliest tornadoes ever to strike the South. The storm moved through residential areas where many homes were not built to withstand violent winds, which made the destruction even worse. In places with dense neighborhoods and limited shelter options, a tornado can cause enormous losses in a very short time. The Tupelo disaster is still remembered because it showed that the Deep South faces serious tornado risk, even though many people often picture tornado disasters as a Plains problem first.

### 5. Gainesville Tornado

The **Gainesville Tornado** struck **Georgia** on **April 6, 1936**, and **killed 203 people**. It tore through the heart of a busy business district filled with workers and shoppers, which helps explain why the death toll was so high. When a tornado hits a downtown area during working hours, the damage extends far beyond buildings. It can shut down factories, destroy stores, injure large groups of people at once, and leave a lasting economic wound in the community. Gainesville remains one of the most severe tornado disasters in the Southeast and a strong reminder of how destructive a big tornado can be in a crowded commercial center.

### 6. Woodward Tornado

The **Woodward Tornado** moved across parts of **Texas, Oklahoma, and Kansas** in **1947** and **killed 181 people**. It remains one of the deadliest Plains tornadoes ever recorded. This storm is often remembered for the way it kept producing destruction across a broad stretch of land rather than focusing on just one town. That kind of long-track damage creates a wider regional crisis because emergency response, medical care, and recovery needs all spread across multiple communities at once. The Woodward tornado also reinforced the danger of a big tornado in open country, where storms can travel far and still strike towns with full force.

### 7. Joplin Tornado

The **Joplin Tornado** struck **Missouri** on **May 22, 2011**, and **killed 158 people**. It showed that even in the modern era, a violent tornado can still cause catastrophic losses when it cuts through a populated city. This big tornado injured over 1,000 people and damaged homes, schools, businesses, and medical facilities across a large section of Joplin. Its impact went far beyond the first day because so much of the city’s daily life was disrupted at once. Joplin remains one of the most important modern examples of how severe tornado damage can overwhelm a community even when forecasts and public warnings are available.

### 8. Amite and Purvis Tornado

The **Amite and Purvis Tornado** crossed parts of **Louisiana and Mississippi** in **1908** and **killed 143 people**. It remains one of the deadliest tornadoes ever recorded in the Deep South. The storm is especially important in tornado history because it reminds people that violent tornadoes are not limited to the central Plains. In rural and wooded areas, the danger can be even harder to judge because visibility is poor and warnings may reach people later. The Amite and Purvis tornado also showed how scattered communities can suffer very high losses when a strong storm moves through places with limited shelter and weaker construction.

### 9. New Richmond Tornado

The **New Richmond Tornado** hit **Wisconsin** in **1899** and **killed 117 people**. It devastated the town and left a deep mark on local history. One reason this tornado is still remembered is that it showed how a powerful storm can turn a smaller community into the center of a national disaster story. A violent tornado does not need a large city to produce extreme destruction. In a small town, damage to homes, shops, public buildings, and basic services can affect nearly everyone at once. The New Richmond tornado remains a strong reminder that tornado risk reaches well beyond the areas people most often associate with severe storms.

### 10. Flint-Beecher Tornado

The **Flint-Beecher Tornado** struck **Michigan** in **1953** and **killed 116 people**. For decades, it was the last U.S. tornado to kill more than 100 people, until Joplin in 2011. The storm hit a suburban area, which made its impact especially striking. Many people tend to picture a big tornado crossing farmland or open Plains country, yet this disaster showed how dangerous violent tornadoes can be in developed residential areas as well. Homes, schools, roads, and neighborhood infrastructure can all be hit in a matter of minutes. Flint-Beecher still stands as a warning that suburban communities are never outside tornado risk.

## How to Prepare for the Next Tornado at Home

After a big tornado, families often find that the emergency keeps unfolding long after the wind stops. A strong home plan needs to cover the few minutes before impact and the long hours or days that follow.

Larger homes **need extra attention** because daily life depends on more rooms, more equipment, and usually a heavier electric load. People often ask what states are in tornado alley in the US, but serious tornado risk is not limited to one part of the country. That is why it makes sense to prepare early, even if tornadoes are not seen as a major local threat.

### Choose the Best Shelter Space Early

A tornado warning leaves very little time to decide where to go. The safest option is a safe room, basement, storm cellar, or a small interior room on the lowest level away from windows. In a larger home, it helps to settle that choice early and keep shoes, flashlights, chargers, medications, helmets, and basic first aid supplies close to that space.

### Use More Than One Warning Method

Outdoor sirens can help, though they should never be the only way your household learns about a storm. Phones, weather radio, local television, and local radio all matter, especially at night or when family members are spread across different parts of a large house. A big tornado can move fast, so losing one alert channel should not leave your home blind.

### Keep Supplies Where You Can Reach Them Fast

Emergency supplies work best when they are easy to grab. Water, shelf-stable food, batteries, power banks, pet supplies, sanitation items, and copies of insurance records should be stored where people can reach them quickly under stress. If your household includes children, older adults, or anyone with medical needs, those items should be prepared with the same urgency as food and water.

### Prepare for a Long Outage

A big tornado can take down lines, transformers, roads, and communications across a wide area. In a larger home, the impact grows because safety and comfort often depend on multiple refrigerators, freezers, internet service, security systems, medical devices, well pumps, sump pumps, garage access, and part of the cooling system. That is why outage planning should include a written list of the loads your home cannot lose. ## FAQs

### Q1: What has been the deadliest tornado in US history?

The deadliest tornado in U.S. history was the Tri-State Tornado of March 18, 1925. It killed 695 people as it tore across parts of Missouri, Illinois, and Indiana. It still holds the highest death toll ever recorded for a single tornado event in the United States, which is why it remains central to every discussion of historic tornado disasters.

### Q2: Is an EF5 stronger than an F5?

**No**. An EF5 is not simply stronger than an F5. The two ratings come from different tornado scales. F5 belongs to the original Fujita scale, while EF5 belongs to the Enhanced Fujita scale introduced later. Both represent the highest rating on their own systems, but the EF scale uses updated damage indicators and a revised method for estimating wind strength.

### Q3: How long can a tornado-related power outage last?

Tornado-related power outages can last anywhere **from a few hours to several days**, depending on the severity of the storm, the level of damage to local power lines, and how quickly utility crews can restore service. In areas hit by major tornadoes, some households may be without electricity for an extended period. That is why large homes often benefit from a backup plan that can keep essential systems running, such as refrigeration, lighting, communication devices, and HVAC support when needed.

### Q4: Should you go to the basement during a tornado?

**Yes**. A basement is one of the safest places to shelter during a tornado because it puts more walls and flooring between you and flying debris. If there is no basement, move to a small interior room on the lowest floor, away from windows. Safe rooms and storm shelters offer even stronger protection when they are available.

### Q5: Should large homes prepare for long power outages after a tornado?

**Yes**. Large homes should prepare for long outages because power loss after a tornado can affect far more than lighting. Refrigeration, cooling, internet service, security systems, medical equipment, well pumps, sump pumps, and garage access may all become urgent needs. That is why tornado preparation for larger homes should include both safe shelter planning and [whole-home backup planning](https://us.ecoflow.com/collections/whole-home-backup-power-solutions).

!Image 1  
  
**The following is a representative list of the most important tornadoes in each state. The criteria for the "worst" in each state is different for each state. In some tornado-prone states, it is strictly based on deaths. In other states, it is based on deaths and injuries. In the states that have never had a tornado death, the selection is made on the basis of damage. Of course, the worst tornado in Nevada is less destructive that even the 500th worst tornado in Texas, Mississippi, or a dozen other states. To give at least some perspective on each state, rather minor events must be included for states where tornadoes are rare. We also change the criteria in 1953. Since that year, forecasting and awareness efforts have drastically reduced the size of single-tornado death tolls in most states. If only the deadliest tornadoes were listed, then few recent events would be included. 
The limitation of space does not allow a listing of every significant tornado. Each state has at least one listing. The listed death or injury total is only for that state, although some caused fatalities in neighboring states. Morning times are emphasized by printing AM in upper case letters. The list of killer and significant tornadoes was derived from the book "Significant Tornadoes" by Thomas P. Grazulis, director of The Tornado Project.**

**The following is a representative list of the most important tornadoes in each state. The criteria for the "worst" in each state is different for each state. In some tornado-prone states, it is strictly based on deaths. In other states, it is based on deaths and injuries. In the states that have never had a tornado death, the selection is made on the basis of damage. Of course, the worst tornado in Nevada is less destructive that even the 500th worst tornado in Texas, Mississippi, or a dozen other states. To give at least some perspective on each state, rather minor events must be included for states where tornadoes are rare. We also change the criteria in 1953. Since that year, forecasting and awareness efforts have drastically reduced the size of single-tornado death tolls in most states. If only the deadliest tornadoes were listed, then few recent events would be included. 
The limitation of space does not allow a listing of every significant tornado. Each state has at least one listing. The listed death or injury total is only for that state, although some caused fatalities in neighboring states. Morning times are emphasized by printing AM in upper case letters. The list of killer and significant tornadoes was derived from the book "Significant Tornadoes" by Thomas P. Grazulis, director of The Tornado Project.**

Damage inflicted by the [2011 Joplin tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Joplin_tornado "2011 Joplin tornado"), the deadliest tornado thus far in the 21st century in the US.

The following is a list of the **deadliest tornadoes in the Americas** including Canada, Mexico, and the United States as well as the countries and islands of the [Caribbean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean "Caribbean") and the countries included in both Central America and South America. While the significant majority of tornadoes on this list [occurred in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornadoes_in_the_United_States "Tornadoes in the United States"), there are also entries for Argentina, Bermuda, The Bahamas, Brazil, Canada, Cuba, Mexico, Panama, and Uruguay.

The [deadliest tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tornadoes_causing_100_or_more_deaths "List of tornadoes causing 100 or more deaths") on record was the [Daulatpur–Saturia tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daulatpur%E2%80%93Saturia_tornado "Daulatpur–Saturia tornado") which occurred in the [Dhaka division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaka_division "Dhaka division") of Bangladesh on April 26, 1989. With a rating of [at least F3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fujita_scale "Fujita scale") from the [World Meteorological Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Meteorological_Organization "World Meteorological Organization") and top winds estimated at greater than 200 mph (320 km/h), the tornado killed an estimated 1,300 people and injured at least 12,000 others. Of all the recorded tornadoes with death tolls of 100 or greater, at least 24 of them occurred in Bangladesh and/or India, and two of them occurred in Europe (in the countries of Italy and Malta).

In the Americas, there are 15 tornadoes on record that caused at least 100 fatalities, the most recent being the [Joplin EF5 tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Joplin_tornado "2011 Joplin tornado") which killed 161 people in May 2011. There are at least 450 tornadoes on record that caused greater than ten fatalities; the most recent of these was the [Somerset-London Kentucky EF4 tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Somerset%E2%80%93London_tornado "2025 Somerset–London tornado") which killed 19 people in May 2025.

Damage inflicted by the [2011 Joplin tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Joplin_tornado "2011 Joplin tornado"), the deadliest tornado thus far in the 21st century in the US.

The following is a list of the **deadliest tornadoes in the Americas** including Canada, Mexico, and the United States as well as the countries and islands of the [Caribbean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean "Caribbean") and the countries included in both Central America and South America. While the significant majority of tornadoes on this list [occurred in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornadoes_in_the_United_States "Tornadoes in the United States"), there are also entries for Argentina, Bermuda, The Bahamas, Brazil, Canada, Cuba, Mexico, Panama, and Uruguay.

The [deadliest tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tornadoes_causing_100_or_more_deaths "List of tornadoes causing 100 or more deaths") on record was the [Daulatpur–Saturia tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daulatpur%E2%80%93Saturia_tornado "Daulatpur–Saturia tornado") which occurred in the [Dhaka division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaka_division "Dhaka division") of Bangladesh on April 26, 1989. With a rating of [at least F3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fujita_scale "Fujita scale") from the [World Meteorological Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Meteorological_Organization "World Meteorological Organization") and top winds estimated at greater than 200 mph (320 km/h), the tornado killed an estimated 1,300 people and injured at least 12,000 others. Of all the recorded tornadoes with death tolls of 100 or greater, at least 24 of them occurred in Bangladesh and/or India, and two of them occurred in Europe (in the countries of Italy and Malta).

In the Americas, there are 15 tornadoes on record that caused at least 100 fatalities, the most recent being the [Joplin EF5 tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Joplin_tornado "2011 Joplin tornado") which killed 161 people in May 2011. There are at least 450 tornadoes on record that caused greater than ten fatalities; the most recent of these was the [Somerset-London Kentucky EF4 tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Somerset%E2%80%93London_tornado "2025 Somerset–London tornado") which killed 19 people in May 2025.

IN MEMORIAM

A. Richard Newton

Dean of the College of Engineering

Roy W. Carlson Professor of Engineering

UC Berkeley

1951 – 2007

> Even those who did not know him suffered a loss on January 2, 2007, when the dean of the College of Engineering at the University of California, Berkeley, A. Richard Newton, passed away at the age of 55. Richard was not only a wonderful engineer and a superb professor but also a great man. He would not rest on the laurels of his (many) industrial and academic successes; rather he relentlessly pursued noble causes that could (and did) have an impact on the human condition. Nothing was too hard for him. He would complain at times and act distressed, but he would never abandon an idea he believed in. Richard liked BIG, audacious ideas, and as soon as he saw a way of making them a reality and in good hands, he would move on to something bigger and better.
> 
> 
> In Chancellor Robert Birgeneau’s words: “An inspired and dynamic leader, Richard understood the power of engineering and technology in entirely new ways, and he connected them to addressing society’s toughest problems. He had an unrelenting commitment to engineering for the betterment of society. His passing is an enormous loss to us at UC Berkeley and for engineering nationally and internationally.”
> 
> 
> Richard was born July 1, 1951, in Melbourne, Australia. As an epitome of the classical ideal of _mens sana in corpore sano_, Richard was an accomplished athlete. He played Australian-rules football in school and then as a semiprofessional; his career was ended by a serious back injury.
> 
> 
> His involvement with electronic design automation (EDA) started way back. A fortuitous meeting in the early 1970s with Donald Pederson, who died in 2004, was to be the event to kick-start Newton's lifelong interest in EDA. In his own words, “In 1970, when I was pursuing my undergraduate degree in engineering, I had the good fortune to bump into Professor Donald Pederson in the computer room of the University of Melbourne, Australia, and before I knew it, I was a SPICE-1 developer.” In 1978, Newton earned his Ph.D. at Berkeley under the guidance of Don Pederson and was appointed to the engineering faculty later that year. Richard quickly scaled the academic ladder, going from assistant professor in 1978 to associate professor in 1982 and to full professor in 1985.
> 
> 
> In his Ph.D. thesis, Richard saw the possibility of developing tools for mixed-mode design where analog and digital components could be developed together. He also intuited that relaxation-based techniques had great promise for metal-oxide-semiconductor (MOS) circuits and developed what was then called iterated timing analysis in collaboration with his students. This method is still the basis of the fast circuit simulators being sold today by the EDA industry.
> 
> 
> In parallel, Richard’s interests evolved to cover all branches of EDA. His main technical contributions in this period were in the field of EDA frameworks, where he spearheaded the development of unified databases and graphical user interfaces for the design of electronic circuits. He was the technical force behind the Electronic Data Interchange Format (EDIF) standard. This work evolved into a sophisticated framework that served as the backbone for the Berkeley EDA team programs and approaches. In 1983, he helped found Solomon Design Automation, the parent company of Cadence Design Systems, Inc., a company that made the ideas of a unified framework for design its flagship.
> 
> 
> It was clear that Richard had a unique gift: he could sense the future and act to direct it. In the late 1970s he saw with great clarity that the computing world was moving towards workstations from big mainframes and that Unix would become the operating system of choice for engineering workstations. He then put his reputation on the line at a very young age and pushed companies and colleagues to join in developing tools and methods on a Digital Equipment Corporation VAX computer equipped with Berkeley Unix. In doing so, he was creating the basis for a new industry and at the same time providing a great test bed for our Berkeley colleagues in the Unix group. Richard had an unmatched talent for marrying technical insights with industrial needs. In these years, he also predicted the great importance of logic manipulation and optimization that led to the formation of Synopsys in 1987. There he served on the board of directors from its inception and had a major role in convincing Aart de Geus, who later became one of his best friends, to try the start-up adventure. He also played an important role in forming other EDA companies, such as Pie Design and Simplex Solutions (both eventually acquired by Cadence).
> 
> 
> After the great technical and business success of these initiatives, Richard moved his interest to the process of enterprise formation. Beginning in 1988, he advised several venture capital firms, including the Mayfield Fund, where he was a venture partner until 2002, and Tallwood Venture Capital, where he contributed both to the evaluation and the early stage development of more than two dozen new companies, including Silicon Light Machines (where he acted as president and CEO during 1994 and 1995), while still teaching digital logic design to an undergraduate class of over 180 students. “Newton had an astute business mind, something you wouldn't necessarily expect from an academic,” said Dado Banatao, managing partner of Tallwood and chair of the Berkeley College of Engineering advisory board. Few people know that he helped found Crossbow with Mike Horton, one of his students, and in doing so, sparked the research on the Berkeley motes, smart dust, and wireless sensor networks.
> 
> 
> In the late 1990s, Richard raised the industrial and academic world to a new level of understanding. He initiated a complex process that led eventually to the formation in 1998 of the MARCO/DARPA Gigascale Silicon Research Center (GSRC), a major private-public partnership with the U.S. government and the semiconductor industry that funds and coordinates long-range research at a dozen major U.S. universities and involves many industrial collaborators. He served from 1998 to 2002 as the founding director of the GSRC. As a consequence of his new interests and acquired skills, Richard served as chair of the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science from 1999 to 2000. In 2000, he was appointed dean of the College of Engineering and became the Roy W. Carlson Professor of Engineering. He served in these capacities until his death.
> 
> 
> During his tenure as dean, Richard was the driving force behind the creation of the UC Berkeley-based Center for Information Technology Research in the Interest of Society (CITRIS), one of four California Institutes for Science and Innovation. CITRIS was established in 2001 to develop the next generation of technologies that will be critical to sustaining California's economic growth and global competitiveness and to solving society's most critical needs.
> 
> 
> In these last few years, Newton became a champion of synthetic biology, seeing the emerging field as the application of engineering principles to the life sciences. He played a major role in the establishment of the Berkeley Center for Synthetic Biology, as well as of the Synthetic Biology Engineering Research Center, or SynBERC, launched last year with a $16 million grant from the National Science Foundation. “The center wouldn't have happened without Rich,” said SynBERC director Jay Keasling, professor of chemical engineering and bioengineering. “He was an incredible supporter and an excellent spokesperson for the center. He could make beautiful analogies between what has happened in high technology and what is now happening in synthetic biology.” Richard Blum, San Francisco financier, philanthropist and vice chair of the The Regents of the University of California, credits Richard for helping develop the concept for the Richard C. Blum Center for Developing Economies, a major multidisciplinary campus initiative launched in April 2006 with a $15 million gift from Blum. “It was his idea that we should use UC’s innovative technologies to help developing countries,” said Blum. “Technology had mainly benefited developed countries.”
> 
> 
> Richard was a strong advocate of promoting women in engineering, and while he was dean, the number of women on the faculty at the College of Engineering nearly doubled from 15 in 2000 to 27 in 2007. Newton also served on the board of trustees for the Anita Borg Institute for Women and Technology, which provides resources and programs to help industry, academia and government recruit, retain, and develop women leaders in high technology careers.
> 
> 
> Richard earned numerous awards throughout his career, including the 2003 Phil Kaufman Award. In 2004, he was named to the National Academy of Engineering, and in 2006, he was named to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. He was also a member of the Association for Computing Machinery and a fellow of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers.
> 
> 
> Outside of academia and research, Newton maintained a strong interest in spirituality and eastern philosophy, formed during his years as a student at UC Berkeley. He also enjoyed poetry (one of his favorite poets being Rilke), painting, and hiking in the outdoors.
> 
> 
> While he had numerous occasions to leave the University for a stellar career in industry or other private academic institutions, his love was for UC Berkeley and its students. Orville Schell, dean of UC Berkeley’s Graduate School of Journalism and a close family friend of Richard’s, said, “Rich believed with a passion that it was the responsibility, in fact the obligation, of a great research university to serve the public by applying its brain power to the problems of people around the world. What he wanted was for all of us to find ways to harness our brains, brawn, money, entrepreneurial energy, research abilities and dedication to solving the problems of our besieged world. Rich was an evangelist for academic relevance. He viewed universities as one of the most important pieces of civil society real estate in our country and the logical locus of innovative problem solving. For him, there was no more appropriate task for a ‘public’ university, such as UC Berkeley, than to serve the public.”
> 
> 
> Richard always acknowledged the role of his students in his career and never forgot to mention their contributions when accepting honors such as the Kaufman Award and in his delivery of the 1995 Design Automation Conference keynote address. Aart de Geus, in his presentation of the Kaufman Award to Richard, wrote: “When asked, though, what he is most proud of, the answer is: ‘my students.’ The common theme among all of them is that Rich was (and is) always there for them and fundamentally was the one that ‘catalyzed’ them to ‘go for it’ and set their talent free!”
> 
> 
> He was a dearest friend to many people. Kurt Keutzer said: “Over the years, I’ve thought a lot about the qualities of friendship: honesty but sensitivity; integrity but loyalty; and most of all, the irrational willingness to go the extra mile. Richard demonstrates all of those. Every one of us has so many stories about how Richard’s big heart reached out to make us happy. But the fact is that Richard wanted to make each one of you happy, in a very personal way, and everything else he did arose out of that.” Richard is survived by his wife, Petra Michel, two daughters (Neris and Amrita), his mother, sister and two brothers.
> 
> 
> > Alberto Sangiovanni-Vincentelli
> > 
> > 
> > Robert K. Brayton
> > 
> > 
> > Jitendra Malik

**2013**

**November-December 2013**

It is the middle of July with the heat index above 100 as I write these notes and wish you all a Happy Holiday Season. Remember that you can read these notes closer to “real time” by going to our class web site:[https://1960.alumclass.mit.edu](https://1960.alumclass.mit.edu/)where Jorge Rodriguez has them posted as soon as I submit them to Technology Review.

Marie and I recently returned from our spring stay in Italy; not wanting to let the grass grow under my feet, I am now packing my bags for a two-week trip to Bogota’.

We received an e-mail from Ted Kraver bringing us up-to-date. Ted has divested himself of the dozen or so activities he had founded or worked with, stopped writing his column for Model Aviation, and decided to “let the world save itself…and create ‘time enough for love.” Ted writes that his wife, Bobbie, is pleased with his decision. In the past year Ted also bought his first luxury car and was selected by the Arizona tech community as a Tech Titan for his twenty years of supporting tech learning in the Arizona schools. Ted and Bobbie were also treated to a grand tour of China by their son and his Chinese wife, going from Shanghai to Beijing to the Great Wall, a trip that included a black chemical snow in Tiananmen Square. While in China, Ted spent $150 on two suits, one a purple Zoot suit from the 1940s, the other an African Campaign British officer’s uniform complete with shorts, knee socks, and Sam Brown belt with cell-phone holster. This past spring included a trip to the Toledo, OH, model airplane show, a Naval Institute meeting in Washington, DC, and an Ed Tech summit in Arizona. Ted was also honored for “my stupid afternoon run in all time AZ record 122 degree heat at 2:46 pm, June 26, 1990.” He continues to build model airplanes, one of them the NC-4, the 1919 seaplane that was the first to fly across the Atlantic Ocean. Ted also thinks that to keep pace with Bobbie’s five degrees, he will work on an MA in military history.

Admitting that he has not been communicative during the past fifty-three years,Joe Rodricks told us what has transpired since graduation. After getting a doctorate in biochemistry, Joe worked for the USFDA on pharmaceutical safety and became a certified toxicologist. After fifteen years at the agency, in 1982 he and four others formed ENVIRON International, a technical consulting company, where he has been for the past thirty years and witnessed its growth to 1500 employees in 90 locations around the world. He thanks his beginnings in Course V for helping with his success. Joe has also published a book on toxicology and risk analysis, as well as a novel,Off Telegraph.Joe continues to work full time and is having so much fun “I cannot consider retiring.” He and his wife, Karen Hulebak, have relocated from their long-time home in Washington, DC, to a farm near Charlottesville, VA. Joe closes by writing, “I would love to hear from long lost classmates.”

Rosaria Piomelli-Ambrosi reports that “[n]ot much is happening in St. Croix, VI, now that the large oil refinery, closed its doors, letting out 10,000 workers. Stores are closing, business is down...the good thing for us is that it is even quieter, deserted beaches, blue seas... a real paradise.”

From David Bleich comes a note opening with “[e]ach year, I am more grateful for having gone to school at MIT. No kidding. It is the best school in the world, especially for people like me who are in humanities.” David continues that he is a senior faculty member in English at the University of Rochester and that “I am very grateful for having gone to MIT and experienced the scientific contexts of our society…. I see how MIT, in spite of its relatively small humanities department, has led the way in teaching the relations between science and the humanities as well as the social and political contexts of science.” David’s new book “The Materiality of Language: Gender, Politics, and the University” remembers the understanding he gained at MIT, including the rise of transformational linguistics during the time we were undergraduates. David concludes with the observation that “[a]t MIT, I did learn to integrate science, society, language, and the humanities. My courses include source material from literature, film, social sciences, history, philosophy, and science. I wish more folks understood how MIT fosters respect for all enterprises in the academy and society.”

Our class president,Dan Whitney, writes that in June he celebrated his 75th birthday, wife Cindy’s 50th MIT reunion, and their 50th wedding anniversary, the last with a family reunion. Dan retired from MIT in January 2012 but continues his consulting. Dan also tells us that, together with the rest of the committee, he has begun planning for our 55th reunion.

I will summarize a message I received from a regular correspondent,Larry Elman.He writes that, despite a recently-broken patella, he was able to walk his daughter down the aisle and share a first dance with her. Larry and Cheryl continue their world-wide hypnosis lecturing. At the awards dinner of the annual meeting of the International Association of Counselors and Therapists, Larry was also honored with the associations Humanitarian Award.

In a recent letter,Richard Greenspan writes that after spending the first fifteen years of his career with Sylvania, he then worked at the Draper Laboratory until his retirement in May of this year. He reports that he is enjoying retirement and looking forward to spending summers at his Wellfleet home. Richard is also considering consulting work in the future.

I close by sadly reporting the death of our classmate Anthony Caserta of Huntington, NY, on June 10, 2013.. In addition to his wife, Elizabeth, Anthony is survived by two children and a sister. After graduating with our class, Tony received an MS degree from The Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn and spent 35 years with Grumman Aerospace Corp., including work on satellite systems, lunar modules, and numerous testing systems for Navy aircraft. Learning the real estate business from his father, Tony was, at 16, the youngest licensed salesperson in New York. He subsequently helped his MIT fraternity, Lambda Chi Alpha, purchase the chapter’s residence. In 1970, Tony also formed Inspecto, Inc., a firm specializing in the inspection of homes for potential buyers and realtors. He also was instrumental in developing properties in New Jersey. Upon retirement from Grumann in 1994, Tony ventured into automotive and marine engineering and developed amphibious vehicles for commercial and private use. For this work and, together with his son, Tony received the Innovator of the Year award from the Long Island Business News in 2002. He was the son of a pianist and was himself a pianist and composer. At the time of his death, Tony was writing a book about music. The class extends its deepest sympathy to Tony’s family, colleagues, and friends.

**September-October 2013**

These notes are one of the occasions when you may have to read about what I have been doing, as I received little from the class.One thing I will note is that the majority of us, born in 1938, have reached the three-quarter century mark. So “Happy Birthday,” realizing, of course’ that we have some who have reached four-score years and others ( including one of this issue’s writers) who have a few years to go.

Jorge Rodriguez, our class treasurer and webmaster, sends us one of his regular reports on the status of our Endowment for Innovation in Education. The figures as of March 31 showed that we had contributed more than $2.0 million to EFIE, which had a market value of $6.4 million, and with almost $2.9 million having been awarded to our faculty Fellows. You continue to outdo yourselves with your generosity.

Dick Bradt reports that he had a great travel year in 2012 as a result of invitations for presentations at international ceramic meetings. Dick spoke on the fracture of refractories at the Brazilian Ceramic Society in Criciuma and then taught a short course on the mechanical properties of ceramics at the University of Sao Paulo in Lorena, Brazil. While in Brazil, he also visited the universities in Sao Carlos and Araraquarra. Later Dick made a presentation on glass fracture dynamics at an Argentine-Chilean Materials Joint Seminar at the Federal University of Santa Maria in Valparaiso, Chile. While in Chile, he had an opportunity to visit the several homes of Pablo Neruda, the Nobel award winning poet. Wrapping up Dick’s year was a trip to Daegu, Korea, for a joint meeting between Japan and Korea on ceramics where he met many old friends from Japan, whom he came to know during his Japan sabbatical in the 1970’s. Dick also taught a short course on mechanical properties at the American Ceramic Society meeting in Daytona Beach, FL in January and reports that it is “always good to spend a few sunny days in Florida in January.” Liz and Dick still live in Tuscaloosa, AL, but one of their daughters lives in The Netherlands and the other in London. Visiting them also provided opportunities for a few European trips to see the grandkids.

We received a short note from Mike Kasser in Tucson, AZ, who keeps as his motto his dad’s favorite Latin quotation, “mens sana in corpore sano.” Following his father’s advice, Mike and Bess went trekking for three weeks to the Mount Everest Base Camp. Mike and your secretary also exchanged a number of notes, as we were searching for some residents of Perugia, Italy, from where your secretary is writing these notes.

A brief message from Peter Silverberg tells us that “I am doing the same things I did in 2010 except getting older one day at a time.”

I am happy to report that, unlike so many issues of these notes, there are no obituaries.

Please write!

**July-August 2013**

Although these notes are for the mid-summer’s issue of Technology Review, I am writing them on a snowy day in late March. I like to give you a sense of the timing, as some of the events mentioned in the notes are completed by the time you read about them.

Among the completed events was the MIT Club of Boston’s May 11 gala to honor MIT’s new president Rafael Reif. Playing a big part in organizing the event were classmates Sue Schur and Jorge Rodriguez.In April Sue also had an exhibit of her paintings at the Somerville Library and is planning a conference in March 2014 on "Architectural Ceramics in the 21st Century: Design and Preservation of Contemporary and Historic Architecture." Sue is working with the MIT Department of Architecture's Building Technology Program, and the Boston Society of Architects' Historic Resources Committee on this conference.

Marc Weiss writes that he is volunteering as a guide and demonstrator at the MIT Museum. He reports that he is enjoying doing the gear demonstration in the Ganson Kinetic Sculpture Gallery. Marc is also volunteering as a tax-aide volunteer at the Somerville Senior Center.

Also from MIT comes word from Richard de Neufville who continues to “commute” to Singapore as part of the MIT team setting up the Singapore University of Technology and Design. Richard also reports that McGraw-Hill has just published the second edition of his book on “Airport Systems Planning, Design, and Management,” which Richard writes is “all you ever wanted to know about airports and more.”

A lengthy note from Jonathan Bulkley brings us up-to-date on his activities since graduation. After completing his SM and Ph.D. degrees Jonathan spent two years on active Army duty, after which he, wife Trudy, and infant son journeyed to Ann Arbor, MI, to join the faculty of the University of Michigan. He retired from the university in 2011 after forty-three years. Jonathan also served as a special master and monitor of the federal court for the Eastern District of Michigan to assist the court in a complex water pollution control case arising from the implementation of the Clean Water Act in Southeast Michigan. Jonathan’s research has focused on water policy and planning, work that has taken him to London, and Shanghai. He credits his time in 1960 in Operations Cross Roads, Africa, installing a water system in Ghana as the beginning of his interest in water policy. Recently Jonathan has also served on the International Joint Commission for the Boundary Waters of U.S. and Canada. Jonathan and Trudy celebrated their 50th anniversary in June 2012. He also writes that “some readers may recall that I purchased a …Land Rover in 1965.One week ago, I sold the Land Rover ….After 47 years with our family, I am very pleased it is going to a good home where I know it will receive proper care.”

Joe Lestyk writes that he believed that he traveled the farthest for our 50th reunion having gone west from California on a trip that took him to Asia and Europe before arriving in Boston. Even though “mostly retired,” Joe travels quite a bit. This year he plans two trips to Europe and one to Australia to watch a cricket test match. On one of his European trips he will be a volunteer with Diverbo, a company that does total immersion English training. Joe says “all I have to do is talk—only in English.”Joe’s travels also have been taking him to Finland and Singapore, where he lived for three years and continues to serve as a company director.

Classmate John A. Tabaczynski, a principal researcher in the Air and Missile Defense Technology division at MIT Lincoln Laboratory, was a recipient of the 2012 Jamieson Award. This award is presented to individuals who have made outstanding contributions to the missile defense technical community. John was presented this award in recognition of his "vital leadership and outstanding contributions to Ballistic Missile Defense Programs."

In a recent issue of Technology Review we reported that Morris Salame was the oldest member of the class. Well,Ed Forys informed us that he is eight months older than Morris. Ed was eighty-one in October 2012. Anyone older? Ed says that the reason for his being older than most of us is that he spent four years in the Air Force after freshman year, and “spent some time bumming around after discharge.”

Doug Bashioum writes that after thirty-six years in the same Virginia house, in 2008 he and Maryellen moved to a 55+ community in NC.Their children, grandchildren, and great grandson continue to reside in Virginia. The Bashioums keep busy with square dancing, and mentoring engaged couples. Doug says that “life is an interesting journey—enjoy each day.”

Bob Mullens writes that he is winding down his second academic career after twenty-one years at Southern Connecticut State University. Bob will continue as an adjunct teaching two courses. With his new spare time he is planning, inter alia, writing a book of children’s stories for his grandkids.

From Larry Elman, one of our regular correspondents, comes word that he will soon become a grandfather for the first time. He also notes that he is celebrating the centennial of his father’s hypnosis research, which included a major event in Zurich. Along the way both Larry and Cheryl became Certified Master Trainers for hypnosis. Both Elmans continue their world wide travels teaching hypnosis. Next year they hope to teach in a number of countries on the Pacific Rim.

A note from Sam Gorovitz tells about a reunion he and his family had with Stuart Brody, ’59. In addition to being friends at MIT, they overlapped at Stanford in graduate school. Sam also writes that this year he was an MIT educational counselor, finally stopping after interviewing thirteen applicants (about twice the normal load). Sam notes that being an EC “is a great way to stay aware of what is happening at MIT – and to reinforce our sense of privilege at having gone to a place few of us could get into these days”.

Finally, I have the sad duty of reporting the death of two of our classmates.

Richard Campbell died in January 2013 in East Weymouth, MA. He is survived by two sons and two brothers and their families. Dick entered with our class and received his degrees from the University of Massachusetts. In addition to teaching political science and writing, Dick was the senior associate for media and public affairs with the Unitarian church in Cambridge. Dick also worked at newspapers in New Jersey and Massachusetts.

James Felix died in February 2011 at his home in Lincoln, MA. For many years, James worked as a software engineer, consulting for Fortune 500 companies. He loved literature and classical music, as well as hiking and bird watching. Jim also enjoyed traveling by train throughout the United States and Europe. He was also an active member of the Rotary Club of Cambridge. James had no immediate family, but is survived by numerous aunts and cousins.

**May-June 2013**

I am writing these notes on Inauguration Day having just watched the ceremonies at the Capitol.

Let me call your attention to our new class website at[https://1960.alumclass.mit.edu/](https://1960.alumclass.mit.edu/).Thanks to our webmaster Jorge Rodriguez, and with assistance from Robert Dimmick, Alumni Association Associate Director and honorary class member, the class web pages have been redesigned and reformatted. We appreciate Robert’s help with the web pages, as we did with all his assistance with our 50th reunion.

I cannot mention our 50th reunion without sadly noting the death in December 2012 of Carl Swanson, chairman of our reunion and class vice president. Carl is survived by his wife of forty-nine years, Ingrid, two sons, four grandchildren and numerous other relatives. Carl resided in South Hamilton, MA, also the location of his company, Swanson Energy Group. After graduating with our class, Carl stayed at MIT and received his Ph.D. in economics and taught at the Sloan School and also served as a consultant to the oil and gas industries. He founded Swanson Energy Group shortly thereafter and continued his energy consulting, as well as serving as an expert witness on both national and international rate cases. In addition to his professional career, Carl also was active in his community, serving as chairman of the United Way of the North Shore and on numerous other civic boards. He enjoyed collecting art, skiing, tennis and golf. He and Ingrid were frequent attendees at concerts, plays, and the ballet. The class of 1960 sends its deepest sympathy to Carl’s family and friends.

Lawrence Kravitz updates us on his recent travels “to remote and distant places, particularly to examine crafts.” Recently Lawrence has visited the Silk Road of China, Mongolia and, closer to home, northern Vermont. At home Lawrence continues his own pottery making and instruction, as well as glass fusion. He also continues his teaching at summer camps and is proud that some of his students have said that he was their inspiration to become an artist-crafts person. Lawrence concludes by noting that his four grandchildren “are proud to wear their MIT apparel at elementary school.”

From Jerry Kaiz we learn that he continues to mentor start-up entrepreneurs in both Montgomery County and Baltimore, MD. Jerry recently received a certificate of merit from Montgomery County for his work in helping new businesses. He recently had his 1960 Plymouth Fury convertible restored and the car has won several prizes. There was recently a tough decision in the family when they had to put-down their long-time companion Airedale, Oliver. Happier times came when they rescued Clover, a four-year old Airedale. The Kaizes attended the 100th birthday of Jerry’s uncle and plan to spend a part of the summer at their Chesapeake Bay home.

This past August Mark Pratt and Suzie celebrated fifty years of wedded bliss with their three children, grandchildren, relatives, and friends. The Pratts divide their time between Naples, FL, (like quite a few in our class) and Westerly, RI. Mark fills his days in Naples volunteering at a soup kitchen and also serves as chair of the client services committee. He also continues to sing with the Naples Philharmonic Chorale. Mark notes that one problem with all his community activities is that he has yet to participate in the meetings of the very active local MIT club. In Rhode Island, Mark serves on the board of governors of the Shelter Harbor Fire District, most of which is on a tidal pond and survived superstorm “Sandy.” He and his neighbors were much luckier than many in the Westerly area where some homes had six feet of sand deposited on them from the storm’s fury.

Dick Oeler reports that he and Elaine took a Danube riverboat cruise from Passau, Germany, to Budapest visiting Vienna and Budapest, as well as other spots in the former Hapsburg lands. This was not a new adventure for Dick, as he had spent much time in Europe in the past fifty years during his work with Air Products, as well as visiting close family in Aachen, Germany. Dick reports that it was the first cruise they had made without family or friends and they enjoyed the opportunity to make new acquaintances. The next trip, a cruise t to Alaska, will include fourteen family members.

The biggest news coming from Tom Farquhar was that he and Barbara acquired a new boat,“Osprey,” and have been working on it to make “each trip a little less of an adventure.”They did spend their fifty-first anniversary aboard her, and did some summer cruising, as well. Tom and Barbara have also been nursing a diabetic cat and, at last report, no longer needed insulin. The Farquhars’ big trip in 2012 was an October riverboat cruise from Budapest to Amsterdam via the Danube, Main, and Rhine rivers giving them a chance to see parts of central Europe with which they were not familiar. “It was an A+ trip,” reports Tom.

In the time since Howard Braun and I had dinner last year during his business trip to Alexandria, VA, he reports that “work stopped being fun so I retired in August,” although he continues his work wih the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board. Howard also has increased his volunteer work becoming an MIT Educational Counselor and providing tax preparation assistance thru the AARP. Howard says he still has a lot of time for bridge and travel.

The past year has been a tough one medically for Bruce Layton. He had a growth in his skull that was treated with a craniotomy at Buffalo’s Roswell Park Cancer Institute followed by radiation treatments, chemotherapy, and extensive rehabilitation. Unfortunately, Bruce had an allergic reaction to the MRI contrast fluids causing swelling that medicine was able to correct. While he still cannot drive, he is back to doing crosswords and Sudoku and will be doing tax returns, as well. We all wish you good health in the months and years to come.

After graduating,Edward Haladay went to Europe on a traveling fellowship for two years, traveling from Morocco to Leningrad and working with architectural and design offices in Copenhagen and Paris. In 1964 Edward joined RTKL Architects and Planners (classmates Ted Niederman and George Pillorge were also with RTKL). Edward became a principal of the firm and spent over twenty-five years there. In 1996 he estableished Edward Paul Haladay Partners, designing residential hotel and resorts in the Caribbean and mid-Atlantic regions. Beginning in 2006 he became active with Habitat for Humanity’s Chesapeake office doing pro bono design work and serving on the board. Edward and Elsbeth have been married for thirty-three years and have two children.

David Powell has retired from active teaching in aero/astro and mechanical engineering at Stanford, but continues to advise a few PhD students. He is also updating his two control system text books, which still leaves him plenty of time for tennis, skiing, travel, and playing with the grandkids.

Our last update comes form Dave Montgomery who in February and March had a exhibit of his digitally stitched panorama photography at a Bethesda, MD, gallery.

**March-April 2013**

I write these notes in mid-November, as Marie and I pack to leave Italy and head back to the States to celebrate Thanksgiving with our family.

By now you should have received a letter telling about the success of our class’s Endowment for Innovation in Education (EFIE). EFIE has been fulfilling its purpose as an important part of MITx, MIT’s part of edX, a cooperative educational initiative among MIT, Harvard, UC Berkeley, and the University of Texas. This initiative is allowing students around the world to enroll in the same courses being offered by the participating universities. MIT continues to expand the quality and breadth of edX, with MIT’s efforts being led by Chancellor Eric Grimson, the latest Class of 1960 Fellow.

An update on EFIE shows that you have contributed $2.0 million, with EFIE’s market value at $6.3 million, and with $2.9 million having been awarded to our Class of 1960 Fellows. Congratulations to everyone for all you are doing to make EFIE the great success that it is.

I will lead off classmate news with an update from Morris Salame who claims to be the oldest member of our class. This past June Morris celebrated reaching four-score years. Morris reports that he is being kept busy renovating the family’s 150-year-old New Hampshire lake house and showing his antique car, resulting in Morris receiving thirty-one awards in 2012. Morris continues to spend February and March in Florida, as he has done for the past fifteen years. He also reports that he has enjoyed meetings of the Cardinal and Gray Society, which gives him an opportunity to wear his 50th reunion cardinal blazer.

From Rudy Marloth comes word that he and his wife have taken up rowing double skulls—he didn’t row at MIT. Rudy also reports that he continues to record the scores of every major league baseball game and now has the score of every game played since 1990. He promises to “some day” do some analysis of the scores. Rudy hasn’t just been recording scores, for over the years he has earned four master’s degrees—EE, ME, CE, and math. To justify all this education, Rudy has been doing energy audits of manufacturing plants. He reports that “my typical recommendation: turn off the compressor when you go home.”

Unfortunately,Tom Christy spent too much time in hospitals this past year. In early 2012 Tom was admitted to University of North Carolina hospital with an abdominal infection that had him in and out of hospitals through August. He reports that after using a walker for a while, he is now fairly ambulatory, although not quite ready to put on the hockey pads and get back on the ice. Tom credits his recovery with keeping in shape from playing organized hockey since 1968—having also played the sport at MIT. Tom added that when he tried out for freshman hockey in 1956, “I was so bad that coach Paul Ronty refused to let me suit up for the first game. Thanks to his patience and coaching expertise, I was skating 2nd line center by the end of the season.” (This brought back fond memories for your secretary who knew Ronty when he played for my hometown Hershey Bears.)

John Beckett currently chairs the Beckett Companies in North Ridgeville, OH, whose parent company was founded by John’s father and recently celebrated its 75th anniversary. John marked the occasion by writing a new book, “Beckett at 75 Years.” Beckett and its affiliates, employs 650 people, including those in two operations in China. Beckett specializes in manufacturing engineered products used primarily in residential and commercial heating. John and Wendy have been married fifty-one years and have six children and seventeen grandchildren. Two of John’s books, Loving Monday and Mastering Monday, tell the story of John’s efforts to bring a faith-based perspective to everyday work.

From Dan Mitchell comes word that he continues to support his favorite charity—no, not MIT—but helping his grandkids get through college. But, Dan also adds, the older he gets the more he appreciates the “doors that an MIT education unlocked for me.” Like many of us, Dan is now a great-grandfather. Dan and Ginny continue to enjoy traveling, with a Russian river cruise being a recent trip and one through Alaska’s inner passage planned for this year .

While Deena Koniver wrote to tell us that she had nothing to tell us, she continues to be very active in her Atlanta synagogue and has recently bought a new home.

Our class president,Dan Whitney, continues his part-time activities with MIT including supervising students in the Leaders in Global Operations program. He also consults with a medical device company and even has a bench in their lab. Dan continues to mentor young engineers and plans to “die with my boots on.”

Recent years have been busy ones for Amadeo Pesce. After retiring from Univ of Cincinnati College of Medicine in 2006, he and his wife moved to San Diego to be nearer their children and grandchildren. Amadeo obtained California certification as a clinical chemist and is now lab director for Millenium Laboratories whose main job is urine testing for pain physicians. Amadeo also edited the ffth edition of the Textbook of Clinical Chemistry: Theory, Analysis and Correlation published in 2010. He also maintains an appointment as an adjunct professor at the UCSD school of medicine. Amadeo adds that his wife has been in an assisted living facility for the past several years.

Also joining the ranks of the semi-retired is John Griffin. He and his wife Nancy have moved from Lincoln, NE, to Jacksonville, OR. John continues to teach an on-line oceanography course for the Univ of Nebraska. John chose Jacksonville, as it is near his Klamath Mountains research area.

I close these notes, as I do far too often, with reports of the death of two of our classmates.

Charles L. Breazeale died October 10, 2012, in Trafalgar, IN. He is survived by his wife Barbara, three children, two stepsons, and other family members. Charles received a chemical engineering degree with our class and then served in the Coast Guard. During his professional career, Charles owned and managed several manufacturing companies, the most recent being Beacon Industries, of which he was the founder and CEO. He also held several patents for his manufacturing innovations. In his leisure time, Charles was a competitive sailor, having taken his Lightning Class sloop to the national championships. Our deepest sympathy goes out to Charles’ family and friends.

Our classmate,Thomas M. Cover, died in March 2012 at Stanford Hospital in Palo Alto, CA. Tom was an acclaimed information theorist and a professor of electrical engineering and statistics at Stanford University. In 1990, the Information Theory Society of the IEEE awarded Tom the Claude E. Shannon Award, the highest honor for lifetime achievement in information theory. Tom is survived by his wife, Karen, two children, a stepson, and four grandchildren. The class extends its sympathy to Tom’s family, colleagues, and friends.

**January-February 2013**

Let me begin this sparse issue of class news with the FY 2012, fourth quarter report on EFIE, our class endowment. There were several gifts near the end of the fiscal year that gave a boost to the totals. Your generosity has reached an impressive $2 million, with EFIE having a market value of about $6.2 million, and over $2.6 million having been awarded to our faculty Fellows.

I don’t know if you saw the statistics on the 2016 entering class, but there are a few differences from those of us who entered in 1956. A quick glance at the numbers shows that 1,620 of the 18,109 applicants were admitted, with 1,138 accepting the invitation and now diligently spending their evenings working on 8.01 problems. Women total 46 percent of the class, which comes from 46 states and 54 foreign countries. Probably the only number that is similar to that of 1956 is the number accepting admission.

Steve Shimberg was the only person who answered my plea for news for this column. Thanks, Steve. Steve writes that he and Orlene are enjoying life on Sanibel Island, FL, from October through May, and are spending their summers in Columbus, OH. Steve and Orlene celebrated their golden wedding anniversary with their kids and grandkids taking a raft trip down the Colorado River through the Grand Canyon. Following that adventure, the Shimbergs then spent a couple of weeks in Tuscany, exploring the countryside around San Gimignano in a Fiat 500. Steve and your secretary also exchanged a few notes on the relative merits of the 500, as well as on some of the highlights of sites in Tuscany, Lombardy, and Emilia-Romagna.

Speaking of travels, your secretary just returned from one of his frequent trips to Bogota’, Colombia, and in a few days he and Marie will be heading to Perugia, Italy, for a couple of months, as we have been doing for the past dozen years.

Marie and I also spent a wonderful few days on Cape Cods visiting classmate Bob Gurnitz and his wife Ellen. We also went whale-watching with John and Debby Christie, both long-time colleagues and friends. John is MIT ’59. We also spent a wonderful afternoon with Reid Weedon, ’41, and his wife Estelle. Reid was Marie’s mentor in the MIT Development Office, where Marie was employed when we met.

Although this column is being written in late September, I am hoping that all had a joyous holiday season and that 2013 will be filled with health and happiness for us all.

I close as I too often do lately with news of a classmate’s death.

Norbert Durando died July 4, 2012, in Fort Worth, TX. He is survived by his wife, Sonja, two children, and grandchildren. His family also included nieces, nephews, and cousins in his native Argentina. Norbert was a graduate of Course XVI and spent his career in the aerospace industry, retiring from Lockheed Martin in 2006. The class extends its sympathy to Norbert’s family and friends.

Frank A. Tapparo, Secretary and Class Agent, 15 S. Montague St., Arlington, VA 22204 E-mail: [ftapparo@alum.mit.edu](mailto:ftapparo@alum.mit.edu)
