**2013**

**November-December 2013**

It is the middle of July with the heat index above 100 as I write these notes and wish you all a Happy Holiday Season. Remember that you can read these notes closer to “real time” by going to our class web site:[https://1960.alumclass.mit.edu](https://1960.alumclass.mit.edu/)where Jorge Rodriguez has them posted as soon as I submit them to Technology Review.

Marie and I recently returned from our spring stay in Italy; not wanting to let the grass grow under my feet, I am now packing my bags for a two-week trip to Bogota’.

We received an e-mail from Ted Kraver bringing us up-to-date. Ted has divested himself of the dozen or so activities he had founded or worked with, stopped writing his column for Model Aviation, and decided to “let the world save itself…and create ‘time enough for love.” Ted writes that his wife, Bobbie, is pleased with his decision. In the past year Ted also bought his first luxury car and was selected by the Arizona tech community as a Tech Titan for his twenty years of supporting tech learning in the Arizona schools. Ted and Bobbie were also treated to a grand tour of China by their son and his Chinese wife, going from Shanghai to Beijing to the Great Wall, a trip that included a black chemical snow in Tiananmen Square. While in China, Ted spent $150 on two suits, one a purple Zoot suit from the 1940s, the other an African Campaign British officer’s uniform complete with shorts, knee socks, and Sam Brown belt with cell-phone holster. This past spring included a trip to the Toledo, OH, model airplane show, a Naval Institute meeting in Washington, DC, and an Ed Tech summit in Arizona. Ted was also honored for “my stupid afternoon run in all time AZ record 122 degree heat at 2:46 pm, June 26, 1990.” He continues to build model airplanes, one of them the NC-4, the 1919 seaplane that was the first to fly across the Atlantic Ocean. Ted also thinks that to keep pace with Bobbie’s five degrees, he will work on an MA in military history.

Admitting that he has not been communicative during the past fifty-three years,Joe Rodricks told us what has transpired since graduation. After getting a doctorate in biochemistry, Joe worked for the USFDA on pharmaceutical safety and became a certified toxicologist. After fifteen years at the agency, in 1982 he and four others formed ENVIRON International, a technical consulting company, where he has been for the past thirty years and witnessed its growth to 1500 employees in 90 locations around the world. He thanks his beginnings in Course V for helping with his success. Joe has also published a book on toxicology and risk analysis, as well as a novel,Off Telegraph.Joe continues to work full time and is having so much fun “I cannot consider retiring.” He and his wife, Karen Hulebak, have relocated from their long-time home in Washington, DC, to a farm near Charlottesville, VA. Joe closes by writing, “I would love to hear from long lost classmates.”

Rosaria Piomelli-Ambrosi reports that “[n]ot much is happening in St. Croix, VI, now that the large oil refinery, closed its doors, letting out 10,000 workers. Stores are closing, business is down...the good thing for us is that it is even quieter, deserted beaches, blue seas... a real paradise.”

From David Bleich comes a note opening with “[e]ach year, I am more grateful for having gone to school at MIT. No kidding. It is the best school in the world, especially for people like me who are in humanities.” David continues that he is a senior faculty member in English at the University of Rochester and that “I am very grateful for having gone to MIT and experienced the scientific contexts of our society…. I see how MIT, in spite of its relatively small humanities department, has led the way in teaching the relations between science and the humanities as well as the social and political contexts of science.” David’s new book “The Materiality of Language: Gender, Politics, and the University” remembers the understanding he gained at MIT, including the rise of transformational linguistics during the time we were undergraduates. David concludes with the observation that “[a]t MIT, I did learn to integrate science, society, language, and the humanities. My courses include source material from literature, film, social sciences, history, philosophy, and science. I wish more folks understood how MIT fosters respect for all enterprises in the academy and society.”

Our class president,Dan Whitney, writes that in June he celebrated his 75th birthday, wife Cindy’s 50th MIT reunion, and their 50th wedding anniversary, the last with a family reunion. Dan retired from MIT in January 2012 but continues his consulting. Dan also tells us that, together with the rest of the committee, he has begun planning for our 55th reunion.

I will summarize a message I received from a regular correspondent,Larry Elman.He writes that, despite a recently-broken patella, he was able to walk his daughter down the aisle and share a first dance with her. Larry and Cheryl continue their world-wide hypnosis lecturing. At the awards dinner of the annual meeting of the International Association of Counselors and Therapists, Larry was also honored with the associations Humanitarian Award.

In a recent letter,Richard Greenspan writes that after spending the first fifteen years of his career with Sylvania, he then worked at the Draper Laboratory until his retirement in May of this year. He reports that he is enjoying retirement and looking forward to spending summers at his Wellfleet home. Richard is also considering consulting work in the future.

I close by sadly reporting the death of our classmate Anthony Caserta of Huntington, NY, on June 10, 2013.. In addition to his wife, Elizabeth, Anthony is survived by two children and a sister. After graduating with our class, Tony received an MS degree from The Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn and spent 35 years with Grumman Aerospace Corp., including work on satellite systems, lunar modules, and numerous testing systems for Navy aircraft. Learning the real estate business from his father, Tony was, at 16, the youngest licensed salesperson in New York. He subsequently helped his MIT fraternity, Lambda Chi Alpha, purchase the chapter’s residence. In 1970, Tony also formed Inspecto, Inc., a firm specializing in the inspection of homes for potential buyers and realtors. He also was instrumental in developing properties in New Jersey. Upon retirement from Grumann in 1994, Tony ventured into automotive and marine engineering and developed amphibious vehicles for commercial and private use. For this work and, together with his son, Tony received the Innovator of the Year award from the Long Island Business News in 2002. He was the son of a pianist and was himself a pianist and composer. At the time of his death, Tony was writing a book about music. The class extends its deepest sympathy to Tony’s family, colleagues, and friends.

**September-October 2013**

These notes are one of the occasions when you may have to read about what I have been doing, as I received little from the class.One thing I will note is that the majority of us, born in 1938, have reached the three-quarter century mark. So “Happy Birthday,” realizing, of course’ that we have some who have reached four-score years and others ( including one of this issue’s writers) who have a few years to go.

Jorge Rodriguez, our class treasurer and webmaster, sends us one of his regular reports on the status of our Endowment for Innovation in Education. The figures as of March 31 showed that we had contributed more than $2.0 million to EFIE, which had a market value of $6.4 million, and with almost $2.9 million having been awarded to our faculty Fellows. You continue to outdo yourselves with your generosity.

Dick Bradt reports that he had a great travel year in 2012 as a result of invitations for presentations at international ceramic meetings. Dick spoke on the fracture of refractories at the Brazilian Ceramic Society in Criciuma and then taught a short course on the mechanical properties of ceramics at the University of Sao Paulo in Lorena, Brazil. While in Brazil, he also visited the universities in Sao Carlos and Araraquarra. Later Dick made a presentation on glass fracture dynamics at an Argentine-Chilean Materials Joint Seminar at the Federal University of Santa Maria in Valparaiso, Chile. While in Chile, he had an opportunity to visit the several homes of Pablo Neruda, the Nobel award winning poet. Wrapping up Dick’s year was a trip to Daegu, Korea, for a joint meeting between Japan and Korea on ceramics where he met many old friends from Japan, whom he came to know during his Japan sabbatical in the 1970’s. Dick also taught a short course on mechanical properties at the American Ceramic Society meeting in Daytona Beach, FL in January and reports that it is “always good to spend a few sunny days in Florida in January.” Liz and Dick still live in Tuscaloosa, AL, but one of their daughters lives in The Netherlands and the other in London. Visiting them also provided opportunities for a few European trips to see the grandkids.

We received a short note from Mike Kasser in Tucson, AZ, who keeps as his motto his dad’s favorite Latin quotation, “mens sana in corpore sano.” Following his father’s advice, Mike and Bess went trekking for three weeks to the Mount Everest Base Camp. Mike and your secretary also exchanged a number of notes, as we were searching for some residents of Perugia, Italy, from where your secretary is writing these notes.

A brief message from Peter Silverberg tells us that “I am doing the same things I did in 2010 except getting older one day at a time.”

I am happy to report that, unlike so many issues of these notes, there are no obituaries.

Please write!

**July-August 2013**

Although these notes are for the mid-summer’s issue of Technology Review, I am writing them on a snowy day in late March. I like to give you a sense of the timing, as some of the events mentioned in the notes are completed by the time you read about them.

Among the completed events was the MIT Club of Boston’s May 11 gala to honor MIT’s new president Rafael Reif. Playing a big part in organizing the event were classmates Sue Schur and Jorge Rodriguez.In April Sue also had an exhibit of her paintings at the Somerville Library and is planning a conference in March 2014 on "Architectural Ceramics in the 21st Century: Design and Preservation of Contemporary and Historic Architecture." Sue is working with the MIT Department of Architecture's Building Technology Program, and the Boston Society of Architects' Historic Resources Committee on this conference.

Marc Weiss writes that he is volunteering as a guide and demonstrator at the MIT Museum. He reports that he is enjoying doing the gear demonstration in the Ganson Kinetic Sculpture Gallery. Marc is also volunteering as a tax-aide volunteer at the Somerville Senior Center.

Also from MIT comes word from Richard de Neufville who continues to “commute” to Singapore as part of the MIT team setting up the Singapore University of Technology and Design. Richard also reports that McGraw-Hill has just published the second edition of his book on “Airport Systems Planning, Design, and Management,” which Richard writes is “all you ever wanted to know about airports and more.”

A lengthy note from Jonathan Bulkley brings us up-to-date on his activities since graduation. After completing his SM and Ph.D. degrees Jonathan spent two years on active Army duty, after which he, wife Trudy, and infant son journeyed to Ann Arbor, MI, to join the faculty of the University of Michigan. He retired from the university in 2011 after forty-three years. Jonathan also served as a special master and monitor of the federal court for the Eastern District of Michigan to assist the court in a complex water pollution control case arising from the implementation of the Clean Water Act in Southeast Michigan. Jonathan’s research has focused on water policy and planning, work that has taken him to London, and Shanghai. He credits his time in 1960 in Operations Cross Roads, Africa, installing a water system in Ghana as the beginning of his interest in water policy. Recently Jonathan has also served on the International Joint Commission for the Boundary Waters of U.S. and Canada. Jonathan and Trudy celebrated their 50th anniversary in June 2012. He also writes that “some readers may recall that I purchased a …Land Rover in 1965.One week ago, I sold the Land Rover ….After 47 years with our family, I am very pleased it is going to a good home where I know it will receive proper care.”

Joe Lestyk writes that he believed that he traveled the farthest for our 50th reunion having gone west from California on a trip that took him to Asia and Europe before arriving in Boston. Even though “mostly retired,” Joe travels quite a bit. This year he plans two trips to Europe and one to Australia to watch a cricket test match. On one of his European trips he will be a volunteer with Diverbo, a company that does total immersion English training. Joe says “all I have to do is talk—only in English.”Joe’s travels also have been taking him to Finland and Singapore, where he lived for three years and continues to serve as a company director.

Classmate John A. Tabaczynski, a principal researcher in the Air and Missile Defense Technology division at MIT Lincoln Laboratory, was a recipient of the 2012 Jamieson Award. This award is presented to individuals who have made outstanding contributions to the missile defense technical community. John was presented this award in recognition of his "vital leadership and outstanding contributions to Ballistic Missile Defense Programs."

In a recent issue of Technology Review we reported that Morris Salame was the oldest member of the class. Well,Ed Forys informed us that he is eight months older than Morris. Ed was eighty-one in October 2012. Anyone older? Ed says that the reason for his being older than most of us is that he spent four years in the Air Force after freshman year, and “spent some time bumming around after discharge.”

Doug Bashioum writes that after thirty-six years in the same Virginia house, in 2008 he and Maryellen moved to a 55+ community in NC.Their children, grandchildren, and great grandson continue to reside in Virginia. The Bashioums keep busy with square dancing, and mentoring engaged couples. Doug says that “life is an interesting journey—enjoy each day.”

Bob Mullens writes that he is winding down his second academic career after twenty-one years at Southern Connecticut State University. Bob will continue as an adjunct teaching two courses. With his new spare time he is planning, inter alia, writing a book of children’s stories for his grandkids.

From Larry Elman, one of our regular correspondents, comes word that he will soon become a grandfather for the first time. He also notes that he is celebrating the centennial of his father’s hypnosis research, which included a major event in Zurich. Along the way both Larry and Cheryl became Certified Master Trainers for hypnosis. Both Elmans continue their world wide travels teaching hypnosis. Next year they hope to teach in a number of countries on the Pacific Rim.

A note from Sam Gorovitz tells about a reunion he and his family had with Stuart Brody, ’59. In addition to being friends at MIT, they overlapped at Stanford in graduate school. Sam also writes that this year he was an MIT educational counselor, finally stopping after interviewing thirteen applicants (about twice the normal load). Sam notes that being an EC “is a great way to stay aware of what is happening at MIT – and to reinforce our sense of privilege at having gone to a place few of us could get into these days”.

Finally, I have the sad duty of reporting the death of two of our classmates.

Richard Campbell died in January 2013 in East Weymouth, MA. He is survived by two sons and two brothers and their families. Dick entered with our class and received his degrees from the University of Massachusetts. In addition to teaching political science and writing, Dick was the senior associate for media and public affairs with the Unitarian church in Cambridge. Dick also worked at newspapers in New Jersey and Massachusetts.

James Felix died in February 2011 at his home in Lincoln, MA. For many years, James worked as a software engineer, consulting for Fortune 500 companies. He loved literature and classical music, as well as hiking and bird watching. Jim also enjoyed traveling by train throughout the United States and Europe. He was also an active member of the Rotary Club of Cambridge. James had no immediate family, but is survived by numerous aunts and cousins.

**May-June 2013**

I am writing these notes on Inauguration Day having just watched the ceremonies at the Capitol.

Let me call your attention to our new class website at[https://1960.alumclass.mit.edu/](https://1960.alumclass.mit.edu/).Thanks to our webmaster Jorge Rodriguez, and with assistance from Robert Dimmick, Alumni Association Associate Director and honorary class member, the class web pages have been redesigned and reformatted. We appreciate Robert’s help with the web pages, as we did with all his assistance with our 50th reunion.

I cannot mention our 50th reunion without sadly noting the death in December 2012 of Carl Swanson, chairman of our reunion and class vice president. Carl is survived by his wife of forty-nine years, Ingrid, two sons, four grandchildren and numerous other relatives. Carl resided in South Hamilton, MA, also the location of his company, Swanson Energy Group. After graduating with our class, Carl stayed at MIT and received his Ph.D. in economics and taught at the Sloan School and also served as a consultant to the oil and gas industries. He founded Swanson Energy Group shortly thereafter and continued his energy consulting, as well as serving as an expert witness on both national and international rate cases. In addition to his professional career, Carl also was active in his community, serving as chairman of the United Way of the North Shore and on numerous other civic boards. He enjoyed collecting art, skiing, tennis and golf. He and Ingrid were frequent attendees at concerts, plays, and the ballet. The class of 1960 sends its deepest sympathy to Carl’s family and friends.

Lawrence Kravitz updates us on his recent travels “to remote and distant places, particularly to examine crafts.” Recently Lawrence has visited the Silk Road of China, Mongolia and, closer to home, northern Vermont. At home Lawrence continues his own pottery making and instruction, as well as glass fusion. He also continues his teaching at summer camps and is proud that some of his students have said that he was their inspiration to become an artist-crafts person. Lawrence concludes by noting that his four grandchildren “are proud to wear their MIT apparel at elementary school.”

From Jerry Kaiz we learn that he continues to mentor start-up entrepreneurs in both Montgomery County and Baltimore, MD. Jerry recently received a certificate of merit from Montgomery County for his work in helping new businesses. He recently had his 1960 Plymouth Fury convertible restored and the car has won several prizes. There was recently a tough decision in the family when they had to put-down their long-time companion Airedale, Oliver. Happier times came when they rescued Clover, a four-year old Airedale. The Kaizes attended the 100th birthday of Jerry’s uncle and plan to spend a part of the summer at their Chesapeake Bay home.

This past August Mark Pratt and Suzie celebrated fifty years of wedded bliss with their three children, grandchildren, relatives, and friends. The Pratts divide their time between Naples, FL, (like quite a few in our class) and Westerly, RI. Mark fills his days in Naples volunteering at a soup kitchen and also serves as chair of the client services committee. He also continues to sing with the Naples Philharmonic Chorale. Mark notes that one problem with all his community activities is that he has yet to participate in the meetings of the very active local MIT club. In Rhode Island, Mark serves on the board of governors of the Shelter Harbor Fire District, most of which is on a tidal pond and survived superstorm “Sandy.” He and his neighbors were much luckier than many in the Westerly area where some homes had six feet of sand deposited on them from the storm’s fury.

Dick Oeler reports that he and Elaine took a Danube riverboat cruise from Passau, Germany, to Budapest visiting Vienna and Budapest, as well as other spots in the former Hapsburg lands. This was not a new adventure for Dick, as he had spent much time in Europe in the past fifty years during his work with Air Products, as well as visiting close family in Aachen, Germany. Dick reports that it was the first cruise they had made without family or friends and they enjoyed the opportunity to make new acquaintances. The next trip, a cruise t to Alaska, will include fourteen family members.

The biggest news coming from Tom Farquhar was that he and Barbara acquired a new boat,“Osprey,” and have been working on it to make “each trip a little less of an adventure.”They did spend their fifty-first anniversary aboard her, and did some summer cruising, as well. Tom and Barbara have also been nursing a diabetic cat and, at last report, no longer needed insulin. The Farquhars’ big trip in 2012 was an October riverboat cruise from Budapest to Amsterdam via the Danube, Main, and Rhine rivers giving them a chance to see parts of central Europe with which they were not familiar. “It was an A+ trip,” reports Tom.

In the time since Howard Braun and I had dinner last year during his business trip to Alexandria, VA, he reports that “work stopped being fun so I retired in August,” although he continues his work wih the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board. Howard also has increased his volunteer work becoming an MIT Educational Counselor and providing tax preparation assistance thru the AARP. Howard says he still has a lot of time for bridge and travel.

The past year has been a tough one medically for Bruce Layton. He had a growth in his skull that was treated with a craniotomy at Buffalo’s Roswell Park Cancer Institute followed by radiation treatments, chemotherapy, and extensive rehabilitation. Unfortunately, Bruce had an allergic reaction to the MRI contrast fluids causing swelling that medicine was able to correct. While he still cannot drive, he is back to doing crosswords and Sudoku and will be doing tax returns, as well. We all wish you good health in the months and years to come.

After graduating,Edward Haladay went to Europe on a traveling fellowship for two years, traveling from Morocco to Leningrad and working with architectural and design offices in Copenhagen and Paris. In 1964 Edward joined RTKL Architects and Planners (classmates Ted Niederman and George Pillorge were also with RTKL). Edward became a principal of the firm and spent over twenty-five years there. In 1996 he estableished Edward Paul Haladay Partners, designing residential hotel and resorts in the Caribbean and mid-Atlantic regions. Beginning in 2006 he became active with Habitat for Humanity’s Chesapeake office doing pro bono design work and serving on the board. Edward and Elsbeth have been married for thirty-three years and have two children.

David Powell has retired from active teaching in aero/astro and mechanical engineering at Stanford, but continues to advise a few PhD students. He is also updating his two control system text books, which still leaves him plenty of time for tennis, skiing, travel, and playing with the grandkids.

Our last update comes form Dave Montgomery who in February and March had a exhibit of his digitally stitched panorama photography at a Bethesda, MD, gallery.

**March-April 2013**

I write these notes in mid-November, as Marie and I pack to leave Italy and head back to the States to celebrate Thanksgiving with our family.

By now you should have received a letter telling about the success of our class’s Endowment for Innovation in Education (EFIE). EFIE has been fulfilling its purpose as an important part of MITx, MIT’s part of edX, a cooperative educational initiative among MIT, Harvard, UC Berkeley, and the University of Texas. This initiative is allowing students around the world to enroll in the same courses being offered by the participating universities. MIT continues to expand the quality and breadth of edX, with MIT’s efforts being led by Chancellor Eric Grimson, the latest Class of 1960 Fellow.

An update on EFIE shows that you have contributed $2.0 million, with EFIE’s market value at $6.3 million, and with $2.9 million having been awarded to our Class of 1960 Fellows. Congratulations to everyone for all you are doing to make EFIE the great success that it is.

I will lead off classmate news with an update from Morris Salame who claims to be the oldest member of our class. This past June Morris celebrated reaching four-score years. Morris reports that he is being kept busy renovating the family’s 150-year-old New Hampshire lake house and showing his antique car, resulting in Morris receiving thirty-one awards in 2012. Morris continues to spend February and March in Florida, as he has done for the past fifteen years. He also reports that he has enjoyed meetings of the Cardinal and Gray Society, which gives him an opportunity to wear his 50th reunion cardinal blazer.

From Rudy Marloth comes word that he and his wife have taken up rowing double skulls—he didn’t row at MIT. Rudy also reports that he continues to record the scores of every major league baseball game and now has the score of every game played since 1990. He promises to “some day” do some analysis of the scores. Rudy hasn’t just been recording scores, for over the years he has earned four master’s degrees—EE, ME, CE, and math. To justify all this education, Rudy has been doing energy audits of manufacturing plants. He reports that “my typical recommendation: turn off the compressor when you go home.”

Unfortunately,Tom Christy spent too much time in hospitals this past year. In early 2012 Tom was admitted to University of North Carolina hospital with an abdominal infection that had him in and out of hospitals through August. He reports that after using a walker for a while, he is now fairly ambulatory, although not quite ready to put on the hockey pads and get back on the ice. Tom credits his recovery with keeping in shape from playing organized hockey since 1968—having also played the sport at MIT. Tom added that when he tried out for freshman hockey in 1956, “I was so bad that coach Paul Ronty refused to let me suit up for the first game. Thanks to his patience and coaching expertise, I was skating 2nd line center by the end of the season.” (This brought back fond memories for your secretary who knew Ronty when he played for my hometown Hershey Bears.)

John Beckett currently chairs the Beckett Companies in North Ridgeville, OH, whose parent company was founded by John’s father and recently celebrated its 75th anniversary. John marked the occasion by writing a new book, “Beckett at 75 Years.” Beckett and its affiliates, employs 650 people, including those in two operations in China. Beckett specializes in manufacturing engineered products used primarily in residential and commercial heating. John and Wendy have been married fifty-one years and have six children and seventeen grandchildren. Two of John’s books, Loving Monday and Mastering Monday, tell the story of John’s efforts to bring a faith-based perspective to everyday work.

From Dan Mitchell comes word that he continues to support his favorite charity—no, not MIT—but helping his grandkids get through college. But, Dan also adds, the older he gets the more he appreciates the “doors that an MIT education unlocked for me.” Like many of us, Dan is now a great-grandfather. Dan and Ginny continue to enjoy traveling, with a Russian river cruise being a recent trip and one through Alaska’s inner passage planned for this year .

While Deena Koniver wrote to tell us that she had nothing to tell us, she continues to be very active in her Atlanta synagogue and has recently bought a new home.

Our class president,Dan Whitney, continues his part-time activities with MIT including supervising students in the Leaders in Global Operations program. He also consults with a medical device company and even has a bench in their lab. Dan continues to mentor young engineers and plans to “die with my boots on.”

Recent years have been busy ones for Amadeo Pesce. After retiring from Univ of Cincinnati College of Medicine in 2006, he and his wife moved to San Diego to be nearer their children and grandchildren. Amadeo obtained California certification as a clinical chemist and is now lab director for Millenium Laboratories whose main job is urine testing for pain physicians. Amadeo also edited the ffth edition of the Textbook of Clinical Chemistry: Theory, Analysis and Correlation published in 2010. He also maintains an appointment as an adjunct professor at the UCSD school of medicine. Amadeo adds that his wife has been in an assisted living facility for the past several years.

Also joining the ranks of the semi-retired is John Griffin. He and his wife Nancy have moved from Lincoln, NE, to Jacksonville, OR. John continues to teach an on-line oceanography course for the Univ of Nebraska. John chose Jacksonville, as it is near his Klamath Mountains research area.

I close these notes, as I do far too often, with reports of the death of two of our classmates.

Charles L. Breazeale died October 10, 2012, in Trafalgar, IN. He is survived by his wife Barbara, three children, two stepsons, and other family members. Charles received a chemical engineering degree with our class and then served in the Coast Guard. During his professional career, Charles owned and managed several manufacturing companies, the most recent being Beacon Industries, of which he was the founder and CEO. He also held several patents for his manufacturing innovations. In his leisure time, Charles was a competitive sailor, having taken his Lightning Class sloop to the national championships. Our deepest sympathy goes out to Charles’ family and friends.

Our classmate,Thomas M. Cover, died in March 2012 at Stanford Hospital in Palo Alto, CA. Tom was an acclaimed information theorist and a professor of electrical engineering and statistics at Stanford University. In 1990, the Information Theory Society of the IEEE awarded Tom the Claude E. Shannon Award, the highest honor for lifetime achievement in information theory. Tom is survived by his wife, Karen, two children, a stepson, and four grandchildren. The class extends its sympathy to Tom’s family, colleagues, and friends.

**January-February 2013**

Let me begin this sparse issue of class news with the FY 2012, fourth quarter report on EFIE, our class endowment. There were several gifts near the end of the fiscal year that gave a boost to the totals. Your generosity has reached an impressive $2 million, with EFIE having a market value of about $6.2 million, and over $2.6 million having been awarded to our faculty Fellows.

I don’t know if you saw the statistics on the 2016 entering class, but there are a few differences from those of us who entered in 1956. A quick glance at the numbers shows that 1,620 of the 18,109 applicants were admitted, with 1,138 accepting the invitation and now diligently spending their evenings working on 8.01 problems. Women total 46 percent of the class, which comes from 46 states and 54 foreign countries. Probably the only number that is similar to that of 1956 is the number accepting admission.

Steve Shimberg was the only person who answered my plea for news for this column. Thanks, Steve. Steve writes that he and Orlene are enjoying life on Sanibel Island, FL, from October through May, and are spending their summers in Columbus, OH. Steve and Orlene celebrated their golden wedding anniversary with their kids and grandkids taking a raft trip down the Colorado River through the Grand Canyon. Following that adventure, the Shimbergs then spent a couple of weeks in Tuscany, exploring the countryside around San Gimignano in a Fiat 500. Steve and your secretary also exchanged a few notes on the relative merits of the 500, as well as on some of the highlights of sites in Tuscany, Lombardy, and Emilia-Romagna.

Speaking of travels, your secretary just returned from one of his frequent trips to Bogota’, Colombia, and in a few days he and Marie will be heading to Perugia, Italy, for a couple of months, as we have been doing for the past dozen years.

Marie and I also spent a wonderful few days on Cape Cods visiting classmate Bob Gurnitz and his wife Ellen. We also went whale-watching with John and Debby Christie, both long-time colleagues and friends. John is MIT ’59. We also spent a wonderful afternoon with Reid Weedon, ’41, and his wife Estelle. Reid was Marie’s mentor in the MIT Development Office, where Marie was employed when we met.

Although this column is being written in late September, I am hoping that all had a joyous holiday season and that 2013 will be filled with health and happiness for us all.

I close as I too often do lately with news of a classmate’s death.

Norbert Durando died July 4, 2012, in Fort Worth, TX. He is survived by his wife, Sonja, two children, and grandchildren. His family also included nieces, nephews, and cousins in his native Argentina. Norbert was a graduate of Course XVI and spent his career in the aerospace industry, retiring from Lockheed Martin in 2006. The class extends its sympathy to Norbert’s family and friends.

## Extract

An essential principle of health posited by the modern Iranian middle class since its rise at the dawn of the 20th century was a strong link between a healthy body and a sound mind. This thesis was built on a reinterpretation of the maxim, ![Image 6](https://static.cambridge.org/binary/version/id/urn:cambridge.org:id:binary:20170221094012316-0384:S0020743805372023:S0020743805372023ffm001.gif?pub-status=live)_aql-i salīm dar jism-i sālim ast_ (a sound mind lives in a healthy body), which drew on modern Western biomedical sciences, specially neurophysiology. Rather than mirroring a simple history of transfer of knowledge (from a creative West to a passive East), this maxim tells a fascinating, multifaceted story of acculturation. Indeed, the general thesis at the base of the present text holds that biomedical sciences were adapted in interaction with problems seen to be created by, and conditions believed to be necessary for, Iran's modernization (_tajaddud_). Shifting the focus of modern Iranian medical history to the intricate interplay between global and internal contexts and forces, this thesis maintains that these interactive patterns were directed at physical, mental, and moral health and disease. They thereby formed a strategy to “medicalize” modernization, addressing its central problem: how to accelerate it without causing social order to collapse, and thus to propel Iran into the ranks of the “civilized nations.” This novel strategy rose in the context of the modern middle class's distress about the chaos surrounding the Constitutional Revolution (1905–11) and the failure of its political focus to advance progress—that is, the belief that change is conditioned on science-driven sociocultural reforms. It was embedded in international colonial structures of scientific knowledge and political power yet, at the same time, was decisively shaped by internal problems. The content of biomedical sciences and medicine was adopted from Western countries. But their contextual objective—the management of modernization—though drawing on late-19th-century Western “medical model(s) of cultural crisis,” was decisively geared to meet Iran's specific circumstances.

## Extract

An essential principle of health posited by the modern Iranian middle class since its rise at the dawn of the 20th century was a strong link between a healthy body and a sound mind. This thesis was built on a reinterpretation of the maxim, ![Image 6](https://static.cambridge.org/binary/version/id/urn:cambridge.org:id:binary:20170221094012316-0384:S0020743805372023:S0020743805372023ffm001.gif?pub-status=live)_aql-i salīm dar jism-i sālim ast_ (a sound mind lives in a healthy body), which drew on modern Western biomedical sciences, specially neurophysiology. Rather than mirroring a simple history of transfer of knowledge (from a creative West to a passive East), this maxim tells a fascinating, multifaceted story of acculturation. Indeed, the general thesis at the base of the present text holds that biomedical sciences were adapted in interaction with problems seen to be created by, and conditions believed to be necessary for, Iran's modernization (_tajaddud_). Shifting the focus of modern Iranian medical history to the intricate interplay between global and internal contexts and forces, this thesis maintains that these interactive patterns were directed at physical, mental, and moral health and disease. They thereby formed a strategy to “medicalize” modernization, addressing its central problem: how to accelerate it without causing social order to collapse, and thus to propel Iran into the ranks of the “civilized nations.” This novel strategy rose in the context of the modern middle class's distress about the chaos surrounding the Constitutional Revolution (1905–11) and the failure of its political focus to advance progress—that is, the belief that change is conditioned on science-driven sociocultural reforms. It was embedded in international colonial structures of scientific knowledge and political power yet, at the same time, was decisively shaped by internal problems. The content of biomedical sciences and medicine was adopted from Western countries. But their contextual objective—the management of modernization—though drawing on late-19th-century Western “medical model(s) of cultural crisis,” was decisively geared to meet Iran's specific circumstances.

The **State University of New York at Buffalo** (commonly referred to as the **University at Buffalo** (**UB**), **UBuffalo**, **UBuff**, or sometimes **SUNY Buffalo**) is a [public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university "Public university")[research university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university "Research university") in [Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo,_New_York "Buffalo, New York") and [Amherst, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amherst,_New_York "Amherst, New York"), United States. The university was founded in 1846 as a private medical college and merged with the [State University of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_University_of_New_York "State University of New York") system in 1962. It is one of two flagship institutions of the SUNY system, along with [Stony Brook University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stony_Brook_University "Stony Brook University").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-6) As of fall 2023, the university enrolled nearly 32,000 students in 13 schools and colleges, making it the largest public university in the state of New York.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-nces-7)

Since its founding by a group which included future U.S. president [Millard Fillmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millard_Fillmore "Millard Fillmore"), the university has evolved from a small [medical school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_school "Medical school") to a [research university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctoral_university "Doctoral university"). Today, in addition to the College of Arts and Sciences, the university houses the largest state-operated [medical school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo_School_of_Medicine_and_Biomedical_Sciences "University at Buffalo School of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences"), [dental school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo_School_of_Dental_Medicine "University at Buffalo School of Dental Medicine"), [education school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_school "Education school"), [business school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo_School_of_Management "University at Buffalo School of Management"), [engineering school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo_School_of_Engineering_and_Applied_Sciences "University at Buffalo School of Engineering and Applied Sciences"), and [pharmacy school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo_School_of_Pharmacy_and_Pharmaceutical_Sciences "University at Buffalo School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences"), and is also home to SUNY's only [law school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo_Law_School "University at Buffalo Law School").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-8) UB has the largest endowment and most research funding among the universities in the SUNY system.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-11) The university offers bachelor's degrees in over 140 areas of study, as well as over 220 master's programs and over 95 doctoral programs, and 55 combined degree programs. The University at Buffalo is one of two universities founded by United States Presidents.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-12)

The University at Buffalo is [classified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Classification_of_Institutions_of_Higher_Education "Carnegie Classification of Institutions of Higher Education") among "R1: Doctoral Universities – Very high research activity".[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-13) In 1989, UB was elected to the [Association of American Universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_American_Universities "Association of American Universities"). The University at Buffalo intercollegiate athletic teams are the [Bulls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo_Bulls "Buffalo Bulls"). They compete in [Division I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I "NCAA Division I") of the [NCAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Collegiate_Athletic_Association "National Collegiate Athletic Association") and are members of the [Mid-American Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mid-American_Conference "Mid-American Conference").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_at_Buffalo&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/Millard_Fillmore_by_George_PA_Healy%2C_1857.jpg/250px-Millard_Fillmore_by_George_PA_Healy%2C_1857.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Millard_Fillmore_by_George_PA_Healy,_1857.jpg)

White House portrait of [Millard Fillmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millard_Fillmore "Millard Fillmore")

City leaders of Buffalo sought to establish a university in the city from the earliest days of Buffalo. A "University of Western New-York" was begun at Buffalo under the auspices of the [Presbyterian Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Presbyterian_Church_in_the_United_States_of_America "United Presbyterian Church in the United States of America") and property was purchased at North Street and College (the site of the later YMCA), on the north side of the [Allentown district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allentown,_Buffalo,_New_York "Allentown, Buffalo, New York"). "University of Western New-York" was chartered by the state on April 8, 1836. Following the charter, private funding was secured for the "Western University," which would endow six or seven professorships at $5,000 each; an addition $12,000 or $15,000 was also collected for a general fund, and a building lot was donated by Judge [Ebenezer Walden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebenezer_Walden "Ebenezer Walden"), one of the wealthiest men in the city.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-14) However, the project collapsed and no classes were ever offered, and only the layout of the College Street campus remains.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-Hough-15)

### Founding

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_at_Buffalo&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Founding")]

The **University of Buffalo** (as it was originally named) was founded on May 11, 1846,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-Hough-15) as a private medical school to train physicians for the communities of [Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo,_New_York "Buffalo, New York"), [Niagara Falls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niagara_Falls,_New_York "Niagara Falls, New York"), and surrounding villages. Future [U.S. President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States")[Millard Fillmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millard_Fillmore "Millard Fillmore"), then a lawyer who had recently served in the [United States House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives"), was one of the principal founders.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-16) James Platt White was instrumental in obtaining a charter for the university from the state legislature in 1846. He also taught the first class of 89 men in obstetrics. State Assemblyman [Nathan K. Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_K._Hall "Nathan K. Hall") was also "particularly active in procuring the charter".[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-Hough2-17) The doors first opened to students in 1847 and after associating with a hospital for teaching purposes, the first class of students graduated the medical school in July 1847. Fillmore served as the school's first [chancellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_(education) "Chancellor (education)"), a position he held until 1874, even as he served in other capacities during that time, including [Comptroller of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comptroller_of_New_York "Comptroller of New York"), [U.S.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_President_of_the_United_States "Vice President of the United States")[](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_K._Hall "Nathan K. Hall")Vice President, and eventually President.

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/62/Pub_Scene_Singing_Alma_Mater.jpg/250px-Pub_Scene_Singing_Alma_Mater.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pub_Scene_Singing_Alma_Mater.jpg)

1907 pub scene, students singing

Initially, the university did not have its own facilities, and early lectures were given at an old post office on Seneca and Washington streets in Buffalo. The first building specially built for the university was a stone structure at the corner of Main and Virginia streets, built in 1849–50, through donations, public subscription, and a state grant.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-Hough2-17) There were continuous expansions to the college medical programs, including a separate pharmacy division, which is now The School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences. In 1887, a law school was organized in Buffalo, which quickly became associated with [Niagara University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niagara_University "Niagara University") just to the north of Buffalo. After four years, in 1891, the law school was acquired by the University of Buffalo as the [University of Buffalo Law School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo_Law_School "University at Buffalo Law School"), which had a downtown Buffalo facility. In the first few years of the 20th century, the university began planning for a comprehensive undergraduate college to complete the basic structure of a university, and in 1909 the university acquired the Erie County Almshouse grounds from the county of Erie, which became the University of Buffalo's initial campus. The establishment may have been influenced by the 1910 _[Flexner Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flexner\_Report "Flexner Report")_ which criticized the preparation of the medical students at the university.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-Why_Innovation_Fails-18) With that additional space, in 1915, the then University of Buffalo formed the [College of Arts and Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo_College_of_Arts_and_Sciences "University at Buffalo College of Arts and Sciences"), creating an undergraduate division in addition to its prior educational work in the licensed professional fields. In 1916, Grace Millard Knox pledged $500,000 (equivalent to $14,794,000 in 2025) for the establishment of a "department of liberal arts and sciences in the University of Buffalo", which was at the time still a private institution. The initial gift of $100,000 was for the purchase of what would become Townsend Hall and the remainder was to establish the university's first endowment, in her husband's name, to support the department.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-A_History_of_the_University_of_Buffalo-19)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/8/83/Early_university_at_buffalo_1900.png/250px-Early_university_at_buffalo_1900.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Early_university_at_buffalo_1900.png)

First home of the Medical College

In 1950, the [Industrial Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_Engineering "Industrial Engineering") department branched off from the [Mechanical Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanical_Engineering "Mechanical Engineering") department. In 1956, a [Civil Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Engineering "Civil Engineering") Department was formed under [Lehigh University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lehigh_University "Lehigh University") graduate [Robert L. Ketter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_L._Ketter "Robert L. Ketter"), who went on to become Dean of the [School of Engineering and Applied Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo's_School_of_Engineering_and_Applied_Sciences "University at Buffalo's School of Engineering and Applied Sciences"), and later President of the university. In 1959, [WBFO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WBFO "WBFO") was launched as an AM radio station by [UB's School of Engineering and Applied Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo's_School_of_Engineering_and_Applied_Sciences "University at Buffalo's School of Engineering and Applied Sciences"), and run by UB's students. The station has since become the launching pad of two modern [National Public Radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Public_Radio "National Public Radio") personalities: [Terry Gross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_Gross "Terry Gross") and [Ira Flatow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ira_Flatow "Ira Flatow"). In 1961, the Western New York nuclear research program was created at the university. This program installed a miniature, active nuclear fission reactor on the university's South (Main Street) Campus. This program was not particularly active, nor could it compete with other government-run research labs, consequently, the programs performed in this facility were abandoned somewhat shortly after its inception. This reactor was decommissioned in 2005 with little fanfare due to material security concerns.

### Acquisition by the SUNY system and second campus

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_at_Buffalo&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Acquisition by the SUNY system and second campus")]

The private University of Buffalo was purchased by and incorporated into the [State University of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_University_of_New_York "State University of New York") (SUNY) system in 1962, and became known as the State University of New York at Buffalo, more commonly known as the University at Buffalo. This acquisition was championed by then-Governor of New York, [Nelson Rockefeller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Rockefeller "Nelson Rockefeller").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-20) As a part of the agreement to merge the university into the SUNY system, the state began to build an extensive second campus for the university. In 1964, the state acquired several hundred acres in the town of [Amherst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amherst,_New_York "Amherst, New York") on the northeast of Buffalo, for development as a comprehensive campus for most of the non-medical disciplines at the University at Buffalo. This is often called the North Campus; it is the center of most University at Buffalo activities. The North Campus project included several major buildings, dormitory complexes, a separate spur of the interstate highway, and a new lake. The undergraduate college, the law school, and graduate schools were all moved to the new campus. During the late 1960s, the [College of Arts and Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo_College_of_Arts_and_Sciences "University at Buffalo College of Arts and Sciences") was divided into three separate schools: arts and letters, natural sciences and mathematics, and social sciences. During the 1998–1999 academic year, the three schools were reunited to re-create the existing College of Arts and Sciences, when the faculties of Arts and Letters, Social Sciences, and Natural Sciences and Mathematics were combined, according to a memorandum issued by the State University of New York.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-SUNY_memo-21)

Since 1989, UB has been a member of the [Association of American Universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_American_Universities "Association of American Universities") (AAU), an organization of 65 leading research universities in the United States and Canada. UB president Satish K. Tripathi serves on the AAU board of directors.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-22)

### "UB 2020" strategic plan

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_at_Buffalo&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: \"UB 2020\" strategic plan")]

Started in 2004 under President John B. Simpson, UB 2020 was a [strategic planning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_planning "Strategic planning") and expansion initiative to develop and implement a vision for the university over the subsequent 15 years.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-overview-23) The centerpiece of UB 2020 was to add about 10,000 more students, 750 faculty members and 600 staff, increasing the size of the university by about 40 percent. UB 2020 also recognized the university's contribution to the surrounding region. The most recent estimates of UB's impact on the local and regional economies of Western New York report approximately $1.7 billion are brought into the local economy from the presence of UB. This figure is also expected to rise by 40 percent, corresponding with UB's institutional growth.

One of the keys to helping UB achieve the goals of the UB 2020 plan, proponents said, was the passage of S2020 and A2020, known as the UB 2020 Flexibility and Economic Growth Act, by the New York State Legislature. On June 3, 2009, the State Senate passed S2020 and sent the bill to the Assembly for their consideration.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-24)

The current president, [Satish K. Tripathi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_K._Tripathi "Satish K. Tripathi"), continued his vocal support of UB 2020[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-ub_2020_overview-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-president_ub_2020_overview-26) and has been actively engaging in campus-wide discussion on the proposed tuition increases introduced by the bill.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-NY_Senate_bill-27)

In 2011, the School of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences received a donation of $40 million from an alumnus, George Melvin Ellis Jr., MD, who earned his medical degree from the university in 1945.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-WGRZ-28) The donation contributed to the $375 million project which has relocated the School of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences to UB's downtown campus.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-UB_Reporter-29) The new school building was designed by [HOK Architects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HOK_Architects "HOK Architects"). A subsequent donation of $30 million from Jeremy Jacobs and family was received in 2015 and the medical school was renamed the [Jacobs School of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobs_School_of_Medicine_and_Biomedical_Sciences "Jacobs School of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences").

From FY2011 to FY2012, UB spent over $300 million on the strategic plan to construct and open four new buildings, including [Davis Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbara_and_Jack_Davis_Hall "Barbara and Jack Davis Hall"), William R. Greiner Residence Hall, the Clinical and Translational Research Center and Kaleida Health medical research building, and Crossroads Culinary Center.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-Davis_Hall_Opening-30)

On August 22, 2013, President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") came to UB's campus to give a speech about needed higher education reform in the country. President Obama highlighted UB's accolades and specifically chose Buffalo for its excellence and commitment to the future, graduation rates and retention, and quality education at an affordable price.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-32)

As part of the UB 2020 initiative, "Heart of the Campus" projects were initiated in phases on each of UB's three campuses. In Fall 2019, UB began construction of the One World Café, an "international eatery" located on North Campus, adjacent to Capen Hall, Norton Hall, and Founder's Plaza.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-35)

Beginning in 2019, UB took steps to distance the institution from Millard Fillmore and ceased its co-sponsorship of his annual gravesite ceremony, due to his [controversial policies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fugitive_Slave_Act_of_1850 "Fugitive Slave Act of 1850") regarding [slavery in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_the_United_States "Slavery in the United States"). A year later, Fillmore's name was removed from the Millard Fillmore Academic Center, and the names of UB's fourth chancellor [James O. Putnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_O._Putnam "James O. Putnam") and [SUNY](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SUNY "SUNY") regent [Peter Buell Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Buell_Porter "Peter Buell Porter") were also removed from campus due to the former's openly racist views and the latter's ownership of slaves.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-40)

## Name

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_at_Buffalo&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Name")]

The university's official legal name is "State University of New York at Buffalo". It is commonly known as the "University at Buffalo" (UB). The institution was known as the "University of Buffalo" for over a century. Other names such as "SUNY Buffalo", "SUNY at Buffalo", and "Buffalo" are also used.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-41) The university's athletic department, particularly on uniforms, uses the name "Buffalo".[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-42)

## Administration and organization

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_at_Buffalo&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Administration and organization")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/14/Clark_Hall_on_UB%27s_South_Campus.jpg/250px-Clark_Hall_on_UB%27s_South_Campus.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Clark_Hall_on_UB's_South_Campus.jpg)

Clark Hall on UB's South Campus

Buffalo is a public university and is one of four university centers of the 64 campuses in the [State University of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_University_of_New_York "State University of New York") (SUNY) which enrolled 467,991 students and employed 88,024 academic staff in 2014.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-SUNY_Fast_Facts-43) SUNY is governed by an 18-member Board of Trustees, of which 16 vote. 15 of the voting members are appointed by the [Governor of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_New_York "Governor of New York") and the remaining voting member is elected by students as President of the [Student Assembly of the State University of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student_Assembly_of_the_State_University_of_New_York "Student Assembly of the State University of New York"). The other two members are non-voting faculty from the University Faculty Senate and [Faculty Council of Community Colleges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faculty_Council_of_Community_Colleges "Faculty Council of Community Colleges"). [Merryl Tisch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merryl_Tisch "Merryl Tisch") is the Chairman of the SUNY Board of Trustees and [John King Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_King_Jr. "John King Jr.") is the Chancellor of the SUNY system. [Satish K. Tripathi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satish_K._Tripathi "Satish K. Tripathi") was appointed by the SUNY Board of Trustees as the 15th president of the University at Buffalo in April 2011, becoming the first international-born president the school has had.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-44) He previously held a six-year tenure as the UB provost and executive vice president for academic affairs. He receives compensation of $385,000, $115,000, and $150,000 annually from each of the university, SUNY Research Foundation, and the UB Foundation respectively.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-45) The University at Buffalo Foundation (UB Foundation) was chartered in 1962 as an independent non-profit corporation and is controlled by a privately appointed board of trustees. It serves as a vehicle to raise private funds for the university, develop real estate, and manage endowment investments on behalf of the university.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-46) The foundation managed a $685.2 million endowment for FY2011.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-47)

UB is organized into 13 academic schools and colleges.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-48)

*   The [School of Architecture and Planning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo_School_of_Architecture_and_Planning?action=edit&redlink=1 "University at Buffalo School of Architecture and Planning (page does not exist)") is the only combined architecture and urban planning school in the State University of New York system, offers the only accredited professional master's degree in architecture, and is one of two SUNY schools that offer an accredited professional master's degree in urban planning. In addition, the School of Architecture and Planning also awards the original undergraduate four year pre-professional degrees in architecture and environmental design in the SUNY system. Other degree programs offered by the School of Architecture and Planning include a research-oriented Master of Science in architecture with specializations in historic preservation/urban design, inclusive design, and computing and media technologies; a PhD in urban and regional planning; and, an advanced graduate certificate in historic preservation.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-49)
*   The [College of Arts and Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo_College_of_Arts_and_Sciences "University at Buffalo College of Arts and Sciences") was founded in 1915 and is the largest and most comprehensive academic unit at UB with 29 degree-granting departments, 16 academic programs, and 23 centers and institutes across the humanities, arts, and sciences.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-General_Information-50)
*   The [School of Dental Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_University_of_New_York_at_Buffalo_School_of_Dental_Medicine "State University of New York at Buffalo School of Dental Medicine") was founded in 1892 and offers accredited programs in [DDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Dental_Surgery "Doctor of Dental Surgery"), oral surgery, and other oral sciences.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-51)
*   The Graduate School of Education was founded in 1931 and is one of the largest graduate schools at UB. The school has four academic departments: counseling and educational psychology, educational leadership and policy, learning and instruction, and information science.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-52) In academic year 2008–2009, the Graduate School of Education awarded 472 master's degrees and 52 doctoral degrees.
*   The [School of Engineering and Applied Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo's_School_of_Engineering_and_Applied_Sciences "University at Buffalo's School of Engineering and Applied Sciences") was founded in 1946 and offers undergraduate and graduate degrees in six departments. It is the largest public school of engineering in the state of New York.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-53) UB is the only public school in New York State to offer a degree in [Aerospace Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace_engineering "Aerospace engineering")[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-54)
*   The [School of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo_Law_School "University at Buffalo Law School") was founded in 1887 and is the only law school in the SUNY system.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-55) The school awarded 265 JD degrees in the 2009–2010 academic year.
*   The [School of Management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_University_of_New_York_at_Buffalo_School_of_Management "State University of New York at Buffalo School of Management") was founded in 1923 and offers [AACSB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AACSB "AACSB")-accredited undergraduate, MBA, and doctoral degrees.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-56)
*   The [Jacobs School of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo_School_of_Medicine_and_Biomedical_Sciences "University at Buffalo School of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences") is the founding faculty of the UB and began in 1846. It offers undergraduate and graduate degrees in the biomedical and biotechnical sciences as well as an MD program and residencies.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-57)
*   The [School of Nursing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo_School_of_Nursing?action=edit&redlink=1 "University at Buffalo School of Nursing (page does not exist)") was founded in 1936 and offers bachelors, clinical doctorate, and research doctorate degrees, along with advanced certificates.
*   The [School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo_School_of_Pharmacy_and_Pharmaceutical_Sciences "University at Buffalo School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences") was founded in 1886, making it the second-oldest faculty at UB and one of two pharmacy schools in the SUNY system.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-Binghamton_pharmacy_school-59)
*   The [School of Public Health and Health Professions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo_School_of_Public_Health_and_Health_Professions?action=edit&redlink=1 "University at Buffalo School of Public Health and Health Professions (page does not exist)") was founded in 2003 from the merger of the Department of Social and Preventive Medicine and the UB School of Health Related Professions. The school offers bachelor's, professional, master's, and doctoral degrees.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-60)
*   The [School of Social Work](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo_School_of_Social_Work?action=edit&redlink=1 "University at Buffalo School of Social Work (page does not exist)") offers graduate [MSW](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Social_Work "Master of Social Work") and doctoral degrees in [social work](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_work "Social work").
*   The [Roswell Park Graduate Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roswell_Park_Graduate_Division?action=edit&redlink=1 "Roswell Park Graduate Division (page does not exist)") is an affiliated academic unit within the Graduate School of UB, in partnership with [Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roswell_Park_Comprehensive_Cancer_Center "Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center"), an independent NCI-designated Comprehensive Cancer Center. The Roswell Park Graduate Division offers five PhD programs and two MS programs in basic and translational biomedical research related to cancer.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-61) Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center was founded in 1898 by [Roswell Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roswell_Park "Roswell Park") and was the world's first cancer research institute.

The University at Buffalo Department of [Media Study](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Media_Study?action=edit&redlink=1 "Media Study (page does not exist)"), located on the North Campus, provides facilities for experimental media production, including video, sound, and digital art studios.

The University at Buffalo is a large, public research university with very high research activity.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-Carnegie-63) In 2020, the university offered 140+ undergraduate programs, 220+ master's programs, 95+ doctoral programs and 55+ combined degree programs.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-65)

The four-year, full-time undergraduate program comprises the majority of enrollments at the university which emphasizes a balanced curriculum across the arts, sciences, and professions.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-Carnegie-63) The university enrolled 21,607 undergraduate and 9,896 graduate students in the fall of 2018.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-Enrollments-66) Women make up 48% of the student body and 78% of the student body is from the state of [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-UnivProfile-67) Over 7,000 students live in on-campus residential halls and 10,172 students live off campus in affiliated housing (including on-campus affiliated housing). Over 79% of students live on campus their first year.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-UnivProfile-67) Undergraduate tuition, room & board, and fees for New York state residents for the 2020–2021 school year totals $24,860 and costs to out-of-state residents totals $42,330.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-68) New York State also offers free tuition for all public college and universities through the Excelsior Scholarship program for families who have an income of lower than $125,000 and are residents of the state. Other requirements to qualify for free tuition include full-time enrollment and staying in the state for a number of years after graduating.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-70)

UB's Health and Sciences Library, Abbott Hall, South Campus

UB is noted for offering an early [Computer Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_Science "Computer Science") major that was distinct from a mathematics major.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-71)

University at Buffalo academic and professional faculty are represented by United University Professions.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-72) The two UUP chapters at the University at Buffalo are Health Sciences and Buffalo Center. United University Professions has over 34,000 members at 29 campuses of SUNY. The organization serves as the collective bargaining agent representing SUNY faculty and professional staff, negotiating contracts and employment conditions.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo#cite_note-73)
